maintopic: NORAD-REPORTED STATEMENT BY SECRETARY GENERAL OF NATO
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in this case my hon. friend has come second, notice of a similar question already having been given by the hon. member for Kootenay West.

maintopic: NORAD-REPORTED STATEMENT BY SECRETARY GENERAL OF NATO
speechtext: With all respect and humility 1 should like to ask the Prime Minister a supplementary question. The Prime Minister mentioned "within a few days". speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Vancouver East asked a question on May 28 which is reported in Hansard at page 578 as follows:
With all parties in this house and people throughout the democratic world paying tribute to Colonel George Flint for his courage, devotion and integrity, would the Prime Minister state whether active consideration can be given to posthumously awarding him the first Canada medal?
There has been no consideration given in this regard. With this description of the service of Colonel Flint, whose funeral is taking place today, all in this house will be in agreement. The Canada medal, as the house knows, was constituted in 1943, but there have been no awards made since that date. Whether or not it can be awarded posthumously, in any event, is a question of some doubt. Apparently the practice has generally been that posthumous awards are dependent

on either statutory or other declarations permitting them to be made. I can say that while I am altogether in agreement that this man performed an heroic and self-sacrificing act, at the moment no consideration has been given to the matter which the hon. member has raised.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Postmaster General. Could the minister inform the house if consideration is being given to adjusting more frequently the rates of exchange on postal orders purchased in Canada to be sent to foreign countries?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for giving me notice of this question. The answer is no, as there seems to be little advantage in doing this. At the present time changes are made each time a variation of one-half of one per cent occurs; and while that may seem a fair sized spread in relation to the practice followed by banks, they are dealing with large sums of money whereas the post office handles foreign money orders of an average value of about $11.25. The change therefore is made each time there is a variation of some 5 to 6 cents in the payment for such average orders. Despite that changes are quite frequent. Last year there were some 24 made in the case of United States orders alone, and on some occasions they have occurred on subsequent days in order to follow the market up and down.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister) moved:
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
That standing order No. 65 be amended by adding the following paragraphs to subsection (1):
(m)	On estimates, to consist of 60 members, 20 of whom shall constitute a quorum;
(n)	On veterans affairs, to consist of 40 members, 15 of whom shall constitute a quorum.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, in making this
motion I direct the attention of the house to the undertaking that was given in the speech from the throne, as follows:
You will be asked to set up a select committee on broadcasting, a standing committee on estimates and a standing committee on veterans affairs, all with power to send for persons and papers.
This amendment to the rules is designed as one of those things which will make parliament, we hope, more effective. The rule in question is standing order 65 (1), which reads:
At the commencement of each session, a special committee, consisting of five members, shall be appointed, whose duty it shall be to prepare and report, with all convenient speed, lists of members to compose the following standing committees of the house:-
The committees are set out and I am not going to refer to them. There has not been

Additional Standing Committees in the past, in my experience, that examination of the tremendous expenditures that parliament makes which is consonant with the degree of responsibility that should rest on members of the house. Billions of dollars come before the committee of supply. With its membership of 264 it is too large to be effective in its examination, too cumbersome to examine in detail the various estimates that are laid before it. That has been the experience not only of successive parliaments in our country but also of the United Kingdom parliament.
I am not going to belabour this question, but I am going to quote from Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, in which he sets forth the situation very clearly and effectively. He says:
Our committee of supply consists of 264 members who can hardly be expected to consider effectively the details of finance. It cannot examine witnesses: it has no other information than the list of estimates, the answers of a minister to questions addressed to him in debate and such casual facts as some private members may be in a position to impart. A body so large and so ill-equipped for inquiry would be a very imperfect instrument for the control of expenditure even if the discussions were devoted entirely to that end. But these discussions afford the only opportunity in the course of the year for the debate of grievances and of many questions of policy. The United Kingdom house seems however to have realized that that practice was not in consonance with the conditions of the day, and it has found a way to make a change without infringing any of the fundamental principles of parliamentary law. They have got around the difficulty by adopting the following course: the estimates when tabled are referred in the usual manner to the committee of supply and they stay there, but a committee on estimates is immediately appointed on a special motion-[DOT]
Then the motion is set out. I continue:
Under this motion, estimates are not referred to the committee on estimates, which could not be done unless they had been previously withdrawn from the committee of supply. Estimates cannot be in two places at the same time. This committee on estimates is ordered to examine the estimates and to suggest economies.
I am sure the experience of members in this house throughout the years has been this; that in so far as the committee of supply was concerned, it was impossible for the house to examine, in that detail that is necessary to bring about recommendations for economy, suggestions for the stopping of waste or improvements in general, because of the size of the committee and also by reason of the fact that it is not possible to examine witnesses. So members of that committee are in the position of having asked questions- and, in general, we have all done this-and made lengthy speeches on various items. The ultimate result was that the estimates placed before the house were simply a record of 
the intentions of the government without there being that examination which would assure economies.
A special committee on estimates was set up and some examination was made in several sessions, but because of the fact that the committee in question had no power to call witnesses before it and examine those witnesses and bring papers before it, its effectiveness was greatly diminished.
One of the major responsibilities of parliament today, as it has been all through the years, is the examination of expenditures in committee of supply. How to control unnecessary and unjustifiable expenditures, without at the same time converting the responsibility of ministers into irresponsibility, is a problem that has been before parliamentarians under our system for many years.
I have said that consideration in committee of supply is not in fact control of the estimates. This is not only my view, it is the view of the select committee in the United Kingdom in its ninth report as far back as 1918. Treasury control is invaluable up to a point, but is not a substitute for parliamentary control. Control by ministers, however effectual that control may be, must on occasion be a control that is insufficient to meet the needs of a meticulous regard for economy.
During days of war we found how effectual a committee could be. There are members of this house who were members of the committee on war expenditures. We had our disagreements in that committee but in general, as one who was a member of the committee for a very long period of time, I found a general desire on the part of members, whatever their position in the house, to deal diligently and effectively with the expenditures that were placed before them without, of course, interfering in any way with the responsibility for policy on the part of the executive.
I know of particular instances in which large sums of money were saved. I recall one occasion when in the examination of certain air expenditures we were able to achieve a saving of many millions of dollars. That is the purpose we have in mind in bringing this amendment before the house. We want to set up a committee of watchdogs whose purpose will be to assure to the greatest possible extent that moneys shall not be wasted and that economies shall be effected.
The experience in the United Kingdom in the operation of an estimates committee has been referred to in a number of textbooks. Some regard it as having been most effectual. Others say weaknesses have been revealed,

that while in general the committee has been successful its effectiveness has been subject to that frailty we all have, that once there is the opportunity to have our curiosity satisfied attendance at the committee is not always as large as it is at the beginning of the session. Jennings sets out the situation in his second edition, 1957, page 303, in these words:
At no time since 1902 has it been suggested that the committee of supply has been an effective means of controlling expenditure, or even a body concerned primarily with expenditure. ... In the main, however, the estimates have been regarded as presented for information, and, as usually happens when information is provided, most members have neglected to inform themselves.
Subject to that-and that is a weakness of all parliamentary institutions, in fact all institutions-very effective work has been done and savings have been effected. In setting up this committee we do so with the desire to make parliament more effective. When we set up this committee we make possible the opportunity for private members, who often do not have that opportunity, to make a personal contribution, one that will pay dividends in the realization of a service performed. To use the words of Basil Chubb in his book, Control of Public Expenditures, it will "stimulate the departments to avoid waste and give the house what is most needed, more knowledge about the conduct of business and a handy weapon for control".
Expenditures today for defence and also to meet the current situation respecting unemployment are and will be tremendous in amount. Our purpose is not to blindfold members but to give them an opportunity, by careful examination consistent with the maintenance of responsibility of the executive, to go into those expenditures that are anticipated in the estimates and in a community of counsel to bring about recommendations which will be helpful in reducing expenditures that are unnecessary or that, as I said a moment ago, are wasteful.
In other words, the setting up of this committee and the submission to it, for instance, of the defence department estimates and those of other departments which are not specifically allocated to existing committees will provide a probing vanguard to the committee of supply. All these estimates ultimately will come back to the committee of supply, but I hope they will have been so meticulously examined that the time of the house will be saved, and economies and savings effected for the people of this nation. The object is to enable members of the house to examine the estimates carefully instead of following the present practice in committee of supply, where we mainly browse through the estimates but do not investigate carefully.
Additional Standing Committees
The only forbidden field, and it must remain so, will be that of government policy. Beyond that and within those limitations which are of the essence of constitutional government under our system, we want this committee when it is set up to apply itself in such a way that whenever there is anything wrong, whenever there is extravagance revealed, whenever there are improprieties that would otherwise remain concealed, the committee will make its recommendations without regard to any other consideration than the welfare of our country.
In other words this is one of the means whereby members of the house will be enabled, if they apply themselves with that diligence which I know they will, to do something to relieve the people of the country from unnecessary expenditures. They will keep departments on their toes if they discharge their duties properly. They will also make parliament a more effective agency than it has been; for after all, changes take place and must take place in parliament to meet changed and changing conditions. The essence of our tradition remains in our parliamentary system, but that system must develop and expand progressively from year to year and from era to era if it is to meet the enlarged field of governmental responsibility and parliamentary consideration.
As far as the committee on veterans affairs is concerned, this constitutes another of the promises made by those who today constitute the government of the country. Over the years we advocated the setting up of such a committee to enable the representatives of the veterans of Canada to yearly place before the members of the House of Commons their views, their recommendations and their suggestions for the betterment of conditions with respect to those who served and their dependants. I am sure this committee, comprised as it will be of members from all parts of the house who know the problems of our veterans, will provide a necessary medium and a closer relationship between parliament and the responsible veterans organizations of our country, to the end that justice and equity to those who served and their dependants will be at all times assured.
Sir, I place this motion before the house, expressing the hope that it will receive general support, and that when this estimates committee is set up the membership of that committee will, in a spirit of self-sacrifice- for it will be that-devote themselves to the tiring, routine but none the less effective examination of expenditures, thereby giving private members of this house a medium whereby they can assist in discharging a

Additional Standing Committees major responsibility of the House of Commons, which is the voting and examination of supply.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this motion I should say at once that the opposition intends to vote in favour of it. But I should like to put on the record certain observations which will give our understanding of the possible effectiveness or otherwise of the changes which are proposed, and which will indicate also certain possible dangers which in our minds, unless great care is taken, may result from these changes. I should like also, Mr. Speaker, to ask certain questions which will no doubt be answered by a spokesman for the government in the course of this discussion.
So far as the establishment of a standing committee on estimates is concerned, perhaps this committee, with its enlarged membership, will now be able to discover some of the $500 million of waste and extravagance which we were told not so very long ago could be easily discovered if a committee of this kind were set up and operated in the right way. If this $500 million of waste and extravagance has already been discovered by the members of the present government, perhaps the estimates which will be referred to this committee would not have reached an all-time high.
So far as the veterans committee is concerned, it has in the past met regularly as a select committee, but as a select committee it was also given the power to ask for persons and papers. The veterans committee, which is now to become a standing committee with an enlarged membership, will be able to secure in its meetings firsthand evidence of the farsighted fairness, wisdom and generosity of the veterans charter which has been developed by previous governments. I hope that in this respect at least we will not be told that nothing happened before the year 1957.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: May I ask the Leader of the Opposition a question? Will he not admit at once that the veterans charter was the result of the work of members of all parties, working very closely together?

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Of course I will admit that without any qualification. I am pointing out that while the veterans charter and veterans legislation received support from all parts of the house, it was the work of previous governments. We have been led to believe in recent days that these previous governments did very little in connection with some other matters, and I am just pointing out that this perhaps will not be said in regard to veterans affairs.

So far as the estimates committee is concerned, and most of my observations will be directed to that particular committee, the motion changes the practice of the house so that the select committee on estimates which has met since 1955 will now become a standing committee. Of course if we follow the normal practice this change will have the effect of enabling the committee to send for papers and persons, and I will have something to say about significance of that particular change later. The motion also increases the membership of this expert and technical committee, because that is what it is and that is how we all hope it will operate, from 26 to 60. Of course this change will cause the opposition certain difficulties, about which I do not complain, especially if steps are taken to have this and other committees sit while the house itself is sitting.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: What is your opinion on that?

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
I think it will be very difficult, Mr. Speaker, for the opposition with its present membership to do effective work on all the committees that will be set up if those committees meet while the house is sitting. Perhaps we will be able to ascertain that as developments occur.
This increase in the membership of the committee on estimates from 26 to 60 has as a purpose, according to newspaper reports, the provision of constructive work for new government members. In that sense, perhaps I can call it a make-work program. We have no quarrel with it because it is good for parliament, good for its membership, to utilize to the full the abilities of all the members. I feel sure that this make-work program will be more effective than some other make-work programs which have been put forward by my hon. friends.
The first motion for a select committee on estimates was made in this house on February 8, 1955, as my friends opposite very well remember. This constituted what was described at the time, and rightly, as an experimental change in the committee system and in parliamentary techniques for ensuring the effective control by parliament over expenditures, which is the primary responsibility and obligation of parliament.
In the United Kingdom-and very often reference is made, and rightly made, to the United Kingdom practice in these matters- the present position in regard to this control was reached after a long history of evolution, of trial and error. I ask, is the standing committee on estimates to be patterned on the British system with subcommittees-I am now talking about the committee on estimates -operating under the authority and direction

of the main committee? Whatever may be the answer to that question, and perhaps we will get it during the course of the discussion, the pattern cannot be the same here as in Westminster, because the British committee on estimates has a membership of only 36 out of a total membership of the house of approximately 750.
However, British parliamentary practices in these matters have been tried and tested. We should not, of course, hesitate to benefit from them, to adapt them, when it is desirable to do so. At the same time there is no reason why we should follow them in every detail. I should like now to express a word of caution, Mr. Speaker, about two related aspects of the change we are now proposing, the extension of the committee system.
I suggest-and I am sure there will be very general agreement with this suggestion-that in making this extension of committee work and putting it on a permanent basis we should be very careful indeed to avoid doing anything which would lead us into the adoption of certain features of the United States congressional committee system.
The whole committee system in Washington is, of course, fundamentally different because the constitutional system there is very different. There, for instance, an appropriations committee can and does propose expenditures itself. But there are other differences than those based on the constitutional structure. It seems to me that very often United States congressional committees-this does not apply to all of them, of course; perhaps we do not hear very much about the committees down there that operate in a different way-act with a maximum of publicity and sensationseeking, with charges and countercharges before television cameras, and in an atmosphere more of party and personal politics than objective, scientific, expert inquiry.
In our system, Mr. Speaker, the most respected member of a committee is surely the industrious, painstaking individual seeking to widen his knowledge and understanding of governmental processes and operations and in that way to make a more effective contribution to parliamentary government, particularly in the bringing about of economies. That approach, based on responsibility and restraint in committee activity, is surely the best guarantee that our committee system, in its now enlarged aspect, will operate with good and constructive results. That has essentially been the British approach in the past, and it is one of the reasons why the British committee system- which has not been above criticism, as the Prime Minister has pointed out-has on the whole worked well.

But we should be making a mistake, I think, if we felt that we could apply the British committee system to our somewhat different parliamentary system. The British committee system, which has so slowly developed, has been broadening down, if I may use that expression, from precedent to precedent. We are certainly not going to be able to adopt that system, even if we were desirable to do so, merely by the passing of a motion of this kind.
As an illustration of the difference between the British committee system and our own, I might perhaps use as an example their public accounts committee, which is very closely related to their estimates committee, as indeed I suppose the public accounts committee here will be closely related to our estimates committee. It has been indicated in the speech from the throne-and we were rather surprised to see this in it-that there may be a change in the parallel committee of this house in so far as its organization is concerned. In the British public accounts committee there are 15 members only, chosen in proportion to their voting strength. That committee meets 30 times or so every session. The chairman of that committee by custom- and custom is sometimes more important over there than law-is always a senior member from the opposition but he is also invariably a financial, banking or accounting expert.
The work of that committee, in so far as I have been able to study it, has always been conducted in a non-partisan atmosphere. Its procedure has been almost judicial and its decisions have always been reached in an expert, technical and objective way. In the twenties, in referring to this committee Sir Austen Chamberlain once said that the public accounts committee operates as a committee of judges putting aside for the time all party considerations, something which is not always so easy, even in committees. Questions asked in that committee are rarely if ever along party lines and the very rare divisions, as I have found from my research into the work of the committee, are never on party lines. The report of this committee is invariably approved by the House of Commons without a division or is not formally approved at all. It is never debated but its recommendations are invariably implemented, even without discussion in the full House of Commons.
The chairman of that committee works in very close collaboration with the auditor general there whose reports are the basis of the committee's work. Indeed, the auditor general sits with the chairman of the public accounts committee. He advises him on the questions to be asked and on the points to be

Additional Standing Committees taken up. He is in a sense a technical and expert adviser to the chairman, and is not himself a witness.
Another difference, in so far as our procedure over here is concerned, is this. With regard to that committee and also with regard to the British estimates committee, the chairman's decision is never overruled because there is no appeal from it. The chairman, the comptroller who is a civil servant, and the auditor general prepare the work of this committee, the accounts to be taken up, which usually are those of the big spending departments, and further items which are advised by the auditor general to be suitable for examination. The other accounts which appear before the committee are usually passed as a matter of routine without discussion.
That committee in Great Britain can call any witnesses it may choose to call, but in practice it nearly always limits its choice of witnesses to the accounting officers of each department, usually the permanent heads, and the ministers are very rarely called. In fact the committee operates in practice, in so far as the calling of witnesses is concerned, in a manner not unlike the way in which our committee on estimates operated here, even when it did not have the formal power to call witnesses. The chief function of the public accounts committee is to ensure that money is spent as parliament intended it to be spent, namely with due economy and with propriety.
I have been mentioning the British system as something that has been tested and tried over the years. But even that system, as the Prime Minister has said, does not operate to everyone's satisfaction in Great Britain itself. When in 1955 we were discussing in this house the setting up of a select committee on estimates the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) in debate on that occasion' had this to say about the effectiveness of the British committee, quoting the United Kingdom auditor general of that time, Sir Malcolm Ramsay. As found at page 967 of Hansard tor February 8, 1955, he quoted Sir Malcolm Ramsay as follows:
The estimates committee has, I am afraid, failed to realize the expectations of those who advocated its establishment. It is true that it has helped to secure certain useful improvements, generally of a minor order, but it has effected no substantial economies and its results have surely been achieved by disproportionate expenditure of time and labour by members and witnesses, and some at any rate of the matters on which it has made recommendations might equally well have been handled by the public accounts committee-
Hence even in Great Britain there is the possibility of duplication of effort with regard to these two committees. Sir Ivor Jennings, who was quoted by the Prime

Minister a few moments ago,-and he is a great constitutional authority in this connection-said that the British committee on estimates was not entirely useless, so perhaps we should not rely too much on British practice in all aspects of committee work in our house.
The other note of caution which I should like to sound with regard to this change was referred to in the debate in 1955, with which my hon. friends opposite will be familiar. They made certain reservations, entertained certain misgivings and sounded certain warnings when they were in opposition, which perhaps might be recalled at this time. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Mac-donnell), who played a very active part in the discussion, had this to say as reported at page 945 of Hansard of February 8, 1955:
-but I wish to repeat that we should be on our guard against its being used

That is, the proposed select committee on estimates-
-as a method to get away from the House of Commons. Ministers being human-
He was referring to us then, but we are referring to hon. gentlemen opposite now.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: But we are different.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Well, you are different, but you are still human. I continue:
Ministers being human, do not let us be sentimental enough to believe, as I said a moment ago, that they do not have that in their minds. Of course it is in their minds.
He then went on in the same debate to quote with evident approval a statement made in the House of Commons at Westminster by the Right Hon. Walter Elliot, a minister of the crown in the British government, in these words:
I am very jealous of any projects to take discussion away from the floor of the house.
This is Sir Walter's view as given to us by the hon. member for Greenwood and as reported at page 942 of Hansard for February 8, 1955. The hon. member continued quoting Sir Walter as follows:
I am uneasy about sending too much to select committees of members specializing on particular matters ... I will refer in a moment to the committee stage of bills, but I would say that the overuse of the specialized committee is a great danger.
There is this possibility of danger, then, and the Prime Minister has adverted to it, that matters may be taken away from the House of Commons by this proliferation of committees which should be debated and settled there. In that same debate and dealing with the same point the present Minister

of Trade and Commerce had this to say as reported at page 966 of Hansard for February 8, 1955:
Those of us who are not on that committee-
He was referring, I think, to the committee on external affairs, which has been operating pretty effectively over the years.
-never have the opportunity to examine the external affairs estimates here in the House of Commons. We have no opportunity of putting questions to the minister. That is all done in committee.
That was not an entirely accurate statement because of course our estimates did come back to the House of Commons and I can recall being examined in the house on those estimates, but that was the fear expressed at that time by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce. To remove the possibility of that happening the hon. member for Greenwood, on that date in the same debate, made a further statement, and I must say I entirely agree with what he said at that time as reported at page 944 of Hansard:
There must be the complete right of debate when the occasion arises in the house referring the items to the committee, and equally the right of debate when the report comes back, as there has been in the case of external affairs.
I mention these things to try to put this change into what I think is proper perspective. In complaining about the effectiveness of committees in the past the Prime Minister in this present session during the debate on the address, on May 13, as reported at page 34 of Hansard, had this to say:
In the past the effectiveness of committees has been nullified because on all occasions the government of those days denied to committees the power, as I said a moment ago. to send for persons and papers.
With great respect, Mr. Speaker, that statement is not in accordance with the facts.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: The standing committees are in that position.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
They are, but the Prime Minister said:
-on all occasions the government of those days denied to committees the power ... to send for persons and papers.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: I should have made it clear that I referred to standing committees.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
If he had said that the statement would have been accurate, but in the form in which it now appears in the record it is not an accurate statement. I would also point out that the select committee on veterans affairs was given power by the house to call for persons and papers. Reading from the order of reference of the committee on
Additional Standing Committees veterans affairs of 1955, under date of Monday, March 7, we find the following:
The committee shall have power to send for persons, papers and records.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: Of course.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: What was the reason the government of that day in so many cases denied the committees the right to call for persons, papers and records? Could he reply to that question? It would be most interesting to hear this revelation.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: I am not familiar with all the details but no doubt we can get them in the course of this debate. However, I do recall that in the case of the select committee on atomic energy the reason was entirely one of security.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: But the others?

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
With regard to the select committee on estimates it was felt at that time by the government and the minister particularly concerned that the committee could operate effectively without running the risk of getting into some of these dangerous areas I have mentioned in connection with committee procedure elsewhere. With regard to the other committees it was felt that the appropriate minister was available. He would have with him in the select committees the officials from his department who could be directly examined in committee by the members. Therefore I am suggesting that in this change in the committee on estimates from a select to a standing committee with power to send for persons, papers and records, the change is greater in theory than in practice.
In any event, Mr. Speaker as I see it the effectiveness of the committee on estimates was not nullified by its inability to send for persons, papers and records, and a reference to the proceedings of the committee over the three years during which it operated would verify that statement. Certainly some hon. gentlemen opposite did pay tribute to the work of the committee during those years, and perhaps in this regard I might refer to a witness of unimpeachable impressiveness and integrity, the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Michener), who had some complimentary things to say about the committee at that time, which I am sure were deserved.
As I understand it, the change from select to standing committee on estimates is hardly likely to be a revolutionary one. Perhaps the change will be most noticeable in the increased membership. When this change from select to standing committee was proposed

Additional Standing Committees in 1956, as it was by hon. members opposite when they were in opposition-and they will recall this-the hon. member for St. Paul's described it as a "very minor" extension of the powers of the committee. He is reported at page 1645 of Hansard for February 28, 1956, as follows:
The proposal introduces a very minor extension . . . because basically the committee will be a committee of the house constituted in the same proportions as the house is with the supporters of the government in the majority and therefore the basic decisions of the committee under the control of the administration.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: Perhaps he was just trying to persuade you to make the change.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Perhaps he was, indeed. He was a very persuasive member in those days, as he is a very persuasive Speaker today.
I suggest that without further changes the basic decisions of the committee on estimates will remain under the control of the government, and I propose to ask certain questions in this regard which may clear up some of my worries with regard to this matter. Who, for instance, will decide what is to be studied by this committee? Will items be selected by the government and by parliament for reference to the committee, or will they be selected by the committee itself; and if the latter, if they are selected by the committee, will the situation in future be that described by the Prime Minister when he took part in this debate on February 8, 1955 and had this to say at page 964. No doubt he will recall his words.
I am not optimistic about its success-
That was the committee on estimates which was proposed at that time.
-for the committee system being what it is, with the committees having an overwhelming majority of the representatives of the government-
The majority will be even more overwhelming in this session of parliament.
_there is no real incentive on the part of the
majority in the committee to permit matters to be brought before it that may be injurious to the government and the party to which they belong.
I recognize the importance of this. The Prime Minister has indicated today that he and his government will not be guided in any way by these considerations in so far as the work of the committee is concerned, but perhaps I may go on to quote the next few lines of the Prime Minister's statement. He said:
Human nature being what it is, I am not saying the situation will be any different under another government.
Well, perhaps it will be different. We will see. The same worry was expressed by the


present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming') when in the same debate he had this to say:
It seems to me that if there is to be a fair experiment on this basis-if we intend to give a fair and reasonable trial to the suggestion-
That was a select committee on estimates.
-which has been seriously put forward in this house over a period of some years, the opposition should have some voice in the selection of the department whose estimates are to go to this committee for review.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Would he suggest now what departments he would like brought before the committee?

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I will not suggest that now; but if the Prime Minister would like to get in touch with me when the committees are set up perhaps I will have something to say on it.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: It is easy to generalize.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: The past master speaks.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
The excerpts I am reading from the debate of 1955 do indeed show how easy it is to generalize without regard to the fact that such generalizations may rise up to cause embarrassment at some future date. In the following year, 1956, the Minister of Finance went a little further in this regard when he said, and I am quoting from Hansard, page 1652:
I say, in the first place, that there is much to be said for the idea of having these particular departments selected by the opposition. In the United Kingdom, the practice in the public accounts committee is to allow the opposition to select the particular accounts or departments which are to be reviewed by the committee.
No reference is made there to the appointment of a chairman from the opposition. Attention is directed to the importance of having the opposition select the departments and the subjects which are to go before the committee. In the circumstances, perhaps there is no need for us on this side to press the present government any further to allow the opposition the right to select the items which would form the basis of the work of this committee on estimates.
In conclusion may I repeat that we will support this motion, but we do not anticipate that it will make any substantial change in the factual procedures which have been followed in these matters since the select committee on estimates was set up in 1955, apart, of course, from giving work to members on the government side whose numbers have been so greatly increased. We will do what we can with the means at our disposal not only to play our part responsibly and constructively on these committees, but to

ensure that any change in committee structure, organization or action which does take place will not interfere with the effectiveness and the rights and privileges of the most important committee of all, the committee of the whole House of Commons.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in the C.C.F. group will support this motion because it contains some of the things we have been advocating in this house for many years, particularly with reference to the appointment of a standing committee on veterans affairs. We are most pleased with regard to this proposal.
We realize that the veterans affairs committee has met in the past as a special select committee. It has met quite frequently and done excellent work, and as to the length and timing of its meetings it has met with the approval of the veterans organizations of this country. However, I feel that veterans generally will consider their position to be more secure when they see that the committee on veterans affairs is to become a standing committee of this house.
As to making the estimates committee a standing committee, we feel that much good could come of this provided certain things are done. We do not think that simply changing the name from select committee to standing committee will necessarily do very much, but if the government is sincere in wishing that the estimates of all departments be examined as meticulously as possible, and if, in consultation with the opposition groups in this house, the work of these committees is to be arranged to this end, we think a great deal could be accomplished. If, on the other hand, this is merely a move, as we have seen it suggested in the press so many times, to give the government's preponderance of members something to do so they may keep out of mischief and so the danger of their embarrassing the government might be partially removed, then we think this may not accomplish very much.
Since this parliament opened we have seen some encouraging signs. Without a doubt, in this session so far there have been more private members on the government side of the house putting forward views which are their own, views which are at variance with the views of the government, than we have seen in many sessions in this house over the years.

speechtext:
Perhaps I missed your point,
but I did say that this session more members on the government side of the house have expressed publicly views which differ from those of their government than I have heard in this house since I came here in 1945. I congratulate those members who have shown some independence of views, because if anything has been noticeable in this house since I am here it is that over the years the government members have been discouraged from showing any initiative; they have been discouraged from showing any imagination and, in words that have been uttered so often by Conservative members in the past, they have had wraps kept on them and have not been encouraged to say some of the things which were nearest to their hearts.
However, I think the opposite current is also noticeable in this session so far. I noticed just yesterday that the Prime Minister himself seemed to view with a great deal of alarm any possibility that members might look on any motion that was voted on as a free vote. The government will be making a very grave mistake in the future if on every occasion they look on every vote as a vote of want of confidence in the government.
We shall see in the days ahead, when these committees are set up, what the government really intends to do. We shall see what the private members on the government side of the house will do in these committees, and I hope there will be less desk thumping in the committees than there has been in the house. I hope there will be less inclination to say that all is well and that nothing needs to be changed. We have had much too much of that in the past. If these committees are set up in such a way and meet at such times as to make it difficult for members to do the work of the committees and of the house, they may accomplish the very opposite to what has been outlined today as the things they should accomplish.
I think the question put by the Leader of the Opposition was most important, when he asked if these committees would be meeting while the house was sitting. He might have asked whether all the committees that are to be set up will be meeting at the same time the house is sitting. I know many hon. members have a great deal of ability, and the Prime Minister is one of them. He has developed that ability in the opposition over a period of many years. I have seen the Prime Minister attend many committee
688	HOUSE OF
Additional Standing Committees meetings during a day, but I have never seen him attend more than one at a time.
Therefore if a member is on two or three committees which are meeting at the same time, and the house is sitting on the estimates of some other department in which he is interested, will this procedure necessarily mean that the estimates will be examined more carefully and that the business of the house will be expedited and more thoroughly considered, or will it be just another way of making it more difficult for parliament to function? What the house must remember at this time is that the opposition is very small in numbers compared with the government members; and if we are to have our time spread over so many committees that may be meeting simultaneously while the house is sitting, will the government's program result in a better consideration of the estimates and of the business of the house?
The whip of this party, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), has just handed me a list of the standing and special committees that are to be set up during the present session, and I have added up rather quickly the total membership of these committees. That total is 713. Perhaps all the committees will not be set up; I am not sure that they will be. Perhaps they will not all be meeting, but to have 713 positions on committees filled by 265 members, with members of the cabinet generally unable to find time to maintain their attendance at those committee meetings, is to demonstrate how very difficult it may be for members to perform their duties on those committees.
I have heard something else, and I am going to say quite frankly that I have not heard it from members generally. I have heard around this building from many people who occupy important positions the suggestion that the session should end very quickly; that it should end in July. When somebody says, "I do not see how it could end before the end of August" they seem to think it would be a terrible thing if parliament sat for three or four months. Well, I hope the government will not set the objective of making this a very short session of parliament. I am not saying that we should make it a long session of parliament.

Mr. Speaker, if we can be certain that the opposition will be given consideration when the government considers the work of the committee, the departments that will be referred to it, and how many of


the committees will be sitting at one time, perhaps the fears that I have been expressing may be groundless and I hope they are. I repeat, it will be impossible for members of the two committees that are now under consideration to be set up as standing committees to do an effective job if the majority in the house is used to keep so many committees meeting that it will be impossible for us to do the work we have to do in this house.
In this connection, members on the government side of the house have expressed rather strong opinions over the years as to the work of those committees. As a matter of fact, in February, 1956, the present Minister of Finance, in relation to the work of one of those committees, had this to say as reported at page 1652 of Hansard:
In these committees, in the case of the public accounts committee, in the case of the estimates committee, indeed in the case of a good many other committees, it is the opposition members on those committees who do the work. Government members as a rule are not interested in probing into expenditures or estimates. It is left to the members of the opposition to do that investigatory work. We have not reached the point here, of course, where the opposition is permitted to make the selection, even in the interests of a strict review of proposed departmental expenditures.
I express the hope that when the Prime Minister asks the Leader of the Opposition what departments he would like referred to the estimates committee he will include, of course, all of the members of the opposition, but I hope he will go one step farther. I hope he will ask the members of the opposition what departments they wish referred to all the committees, because surely it is a very important consideration whether or not the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, for example, are to be referred to a committee; whether the estimates of other departments of the government are to be referred to other committees, since it is possible for a number of committees meeting at the same time to be dealing with estimates of departments but not the estimates committee itself.
The members of the C.C.F. group are here, Mr. Speaker, as I believe other members are here, to make parliament most effective. We hope that whatever is done the work of the committee of supply and of the house will be kept to the forefront, and that the work of these other committees will only be used to help the committee of supply and the house so that parliament may maintain solid control over the passage of the estimates, and so that members in fact may be able to use their time to the best advantage.

There is something else that was very dear to the Prime Minister when he was in opposition with respect to the work of members in committees and in the house. That was his feeling that members on both sides of the house should have research help made available to them so they could get the facts necessary to do an efficient job in committees or in the house. I express the hope that during this parliament, when opposition members are reduced in number and when committee work is being expanded very greatly, the Prime Minister and the cabinet will consider the oft-repeated suggestion of the Prime Minister himself in former years that adequate research assistance should be made available to all members of the house.

My recollection of the reason for setting up the war expenditures committee in 1941-I think the Prime Minister will agree with me on this-is that there were no estimates of the vast war expenditures. There was merely one war appropriation bill with one item in it, and the basic problem that arose then was the inability of hon. members to get anything in the nature of estimates to cover those vast expenditures. There was another reason for setting up the war expenditures committee, namely that to a considerable extent the expenditures concerned security matters and there was a problem involved in giving certain details of information in the House of Commons that one would ordinarily expect to be given in the case of expenditures. For that reason many of the sittings of the war expenditures committee were in camera.

I hold the view that to the greatest extent possible estimates should be dealt with in the House of Commons. I do not want this estimates committee to become a substitute for the committee of supply. I think we must be careful about that.
A lot of things have been said about keeping busy the vast army of new young members supporting the government. Perhaps it is not necessary to comment too much on that, but I hope the estimates committee will not become merely a committee of study for those hon. members in order to keep them busy. There is a real danger of that happening.
I would hope that care would be taken to see that it does not happen, because if that were to happen it would tend to lessen the effectiveness of the committee of supply on estimates. I believe that is an undesirable thing. I am old-fashioned enough to believe very strongly that control of expenditures by the House of Commons is very basic to our system, and something we must carefully preserve by all possible means.
Another interesting feature about embalming this new subsection (m) in standing order 65 is this; it prevents debate on this subject each year. I am not sure that in the last three years during which the special committee on estimates has been set up the experience gained has been sufficiently great to warrant taking the subject matter we are now debating out of the House of Commons. In other words it is probably a good thing to have a motion to set up the special committee brought before the house for debate each year, at least until we get a bit more experience on the subject. I want to raise two other points, one of which is in connection with this whole matter of committees sitting while the house is in session. This is a new practice which has been adopted within the last few years. I recall well that when such a request was first made by committees there was always a debate on it and an explanation by the person putting forward the request. All I am saying now is that if it is going to become the practice, I hope great care will be taken by the government to not ask that committees sit while the house is sitting unless there is some special need for it, as there is when the Canadian National report is before the committee on railways and shipping, and as there is when the wheat board report is before the committee on agriculture. I hope, however, it will not become the general practice to permit committees to sit while the house is sitting, because that is not a good departure.

I happen to have been the first minister-
I do not know whether I should say victim -who appeared before the estimates committee when it was set up for the first time by this house in 1955. As a result of my experience, at that time I formed certain impressions about that committee, about the way in which it could function effectively and about certain ways in which I did not think it could function effectively.
I do not think the Prime Minister, when he introduced the motion today, was altogether clear in his own mind as to precisely what function this committee could really be expected to perform. I am not surprised, and this is not meant as criticism. Unless I am mistaken, one of the reasons is that the Prime Minister himself was never a member of the committee and had no direct experience of its working. Of course, until certain regrettable events last June, the Prime Minister had never sat on the treasury benches and therefore had looked at the committee from only one side of the house. I can now look at it, perhaps without too much enthusiasm, from both sides.
In the consideration of the estimates in the house or in the committee-and I tried to think this matter over during the lunch hour-it seemed to me that there were four possible objectives which hon. members might have in mind. The first is one that was traditional in the days when parliament really represented the taxpayers against the crown and when the purpose of parliament was to keep down expenditures-and that was a long time ago, Mr. Speaker-when the purpose of examining the estimates was to see whether any unnecessary demand by the crown could not be cut down. I am afraid that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green), who has been here as long as have most of us in this house and who sat on this side of the house for a long time,-

Oh, they were all for reducing the total but never any of the elements that made up the total. In what I am saying, I am merely reflecting what men of great experience have said in this house on more than one occasion. I am sure the Minister of Public Works will recall occasions when Mr. Ilsley and Mr. Abbott pointed out that they felt that they were the only members of the house,-they did not include even their colleagues-when they were in the position of minister of finance, who were really interested in economies. I do not think there is any more likelihood of getting any effective reduction of the estimates from the estimates committee than there is from the committee of supply of this house. The fact of the matter is that under modern conditions the taxpayer is an anonymous person but the people who are advocating expenditures are certainly not anonymous and are often extremely vocal. The pressure in modern times on all members of parliament, wherever they may sit in this house, is for more and more, not less and less expenditure. I recall my own experience in the estimates committee. As a matter of fact, I had a sneaking feeling that some of the expenditures being made by my department when I was the minister were unnecessary.
I had certain hopes when my estimates went before the committee. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, because you were a member of that committee, how frank the officials were and how more than frank I was at times in answering every question put by members of the committee. You will recall that far from any suggestion being made that there should be any reduction in expenditures, quite a number of suggestions were made that expenditures should be increased.

speechtext:
That is exactly what I was alluding to. The second purpose that hon. members may have in mind in considering


the estimates either in committee in this place or in a special committee or a standing committee, is to secure information. For this purpose I think the committee is admirable. There are many hon. members who are not particularly interested, and properly so because none of us can hope to encompass all the encyclopaedic matters that come before this parliament, in the details of this or that department. If all the estimates are going to be considered in all their details in this place, it means that little discussions with perhaps 15 people or 20 people on one side of the house and a similar number on the other will go on for great lengths of time. As the Prime Minister, I thought wisely and properly, pointed out this morning, the objective could be much better achieved in another place in a smaller committee to the satisfaction of the members particularly interested. I think that perhaps the most useful function the estimates committee can perform is that of providing this information in detail-I refer to information about detailed and specialized sides of the manifold activities of government that can be given in the committee-with the time of the vast majority of members who are not and need not be especially interested in it being thereby saved to the end that other and more important business can be transacted in this place.
Then there is another purpose that hon. members have in taking part in the discussions in the committee of supply. That purpose is to make representations on behalf of their constituents about the activities of departments and agencies of government. I would hope that there would be some members who would feel content to make those representations in the relative obscurity of the estimates committee. I would also hope that the estimates committee would be relatively obscure. But I do not think the Prime Minister ought to cherish the hope that that would be done by very many members. The average member who wishes to make representations on behalf of his constituents-and I am afraid I must admit that I am no exception-wants to make them in this place so that they will be on Hansard and will be readily accessible to his constituents. That is an understandable attitude. I do not think that we shall ever get that function performed in any committee, however large and however much spotlight there may be upon it.
Then there is the fourth purpose of the consideration of the estimates, and that is to discuss the policies of the various departments. I know that no hard and fast line can be drawn between policy and administration and that in the committee, or in the committee of supply, that line is often going to be crossed unconsciously, but I do think that

what we ought to aim for in relation to this committee is to have the discussion of policy of departments here in the committee of supply and to have the discussion of administration and the seeking of information about administration as largely as possible in the estimates committee. That is an ideal which could probably never be reached.
In the experience of the past three years I do not think a great deal of time has been saved by having a committee on estimates, but I believe the discussion of the departments which went to the estimates committee was very materially improved here in the committee of supply later on because of the preliminary investigation in the estimates committee. I feel that, over the years, if hon. members take their duties in the committee conscientiously that would increasingly be the case.
I was extremely pleased to hear-and as my leader was, I too am very much in accord with it-what the Prime Minister said about ministerial responsibility and the obligation of keeping the responsibility for policy in the ministry and excepting policy questions from the purview of the committee. This is the view which I took when I first appeared before the committee at its very first session at the beginning of the proceedings in 1955, I set out the position of ministerial responsibility that was then taken and I am happy to say that there was no real dissent in the committee from that position.
There is a problem about having the estimates considered in a committee and having civil servants speak directly in reply to questions. That problem was discussed at the first meeting of the committee. I believe that either a minister or a parliamentary assistant ought always to be present at the committee. In my view it is wrong under our system to leave civil servants in the exposed position of having to discriminate between policy questions and questions of administration. Perhaps I say that because I was once a civil servant myself, but nevertheless I think we all have a duty, and the government has a special duty, to see that this is not done. I make that statement because oppositions have a temptation, which I think hon. gentlemen opposite having recently been here will recall, to try to find some contradictions between ministers and their officials, which is perhaps part of that human nature about which we heard so much earlier in this debate. It is really the duty of the minister to see that civil servants are not exposed to that temptation and are not dragged into political controversies. That is very apt to happen unless either the minister or his parliamentary assistant is present in the committee to intervene when questions are asked and to say,
Additional Standing Committees "That is my responsibility and I must accept the responsibility for answering."
Perhaps because some of us on this side of the house recently had ministerial responsibility there will not be so much disposition to cross that line as there might have been at some other time. It is a special responsibility of the government to see that the line is not crossed and of course the discharge of that duty is sometimes open to misinterpretation. Our conduct in this respect while we were in office was quite often misinterpreted. We were often accused of withholding information because we insisted upon giving the answers ourselves, as ministers, instead of having the answers given by officials, when our only motive in giving the answers ourselves was to take the responsibility which under the British system was inescapably ours.
I was reassured to hear the Prime Minister say what he said today about the importance of emphasizing that position. The Prime Minister asked the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) why it was that in the case of this committee, when it was originally set up, the government of the day decided not to give the committee power to send for persons and papers. Perhaps I might amplify what the Leader of the Opposition said because that matter was discussed directly with me by the then prime minister and the then minister of finance before I went into the committee and I can assure the house it was not through any desire to deny any hon. member of the house any information about the work of the department that he might seek to get.
There was a feeling that the purpose of this committee was to be a "mirror in little", if I may put it that way, of the committee of supply, and we do not call witnesses in the committee of supply and we do have civil servants sit in front of the minister to assist him in giving the answers. It was thought that the only deviation which should be made from that course in order to focus attention on the estimates themselves was that the ministers at their discretion might permit the civil servants to speak directly. There was a feeling that if civil servants appeared as witnesses rather than to assist the minister, there might be an impression created that they were compelled to answer questions which it would not be proper for civil servants to answer. I do not think this is a big point. Indeed, it may be that it was an unnecessary fear.
