maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Perhaps I have not been in opposition long enough to have achieved the point of view that one should exploit every advantage possible against the government. Perhaps I still have clinging to me some of the attitudes I had when I sat on the other side of the house. I hope not, but perhaps I have.
I hope it is not contemplated by the Prime Minister or the government that the estimates committee is going to be calling witnesses from the general public. It seems to me that if that course is ever followed it should be a highly exceptional proceeding. If this committee is to do work that would otherwise be done by the committee of supply, and do it efficiently, they will have all their time taken up examining officials of the departments and agencies of the government which directly have to do with the administration. It is difficult to conceive of circumstances, though they might arise, in which it would really be desirable to go beyond that except for the purpose of seeking to create some kind of sensation. I agree completely that we do not want to have develop in Canada the type of committee that is found in the United States congress. I trust there will be no thought of having the proceedings of the committee televised and that it will be free of all the apparatus which accompanies committee meetings in some other jurisdictions.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: I would have thought your party had had enough television.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
The Prime Minister in his remarks this morning referred to the war expenditures committee of which he was a distinguished member between 1940 and 1945. I was a civil servant in those days but I occasionally sat in the galleries of this house and followed its proceedings with a certain detached interest. I am not sure that the Prime Minister, though he did not say so, did not really give away the real reason why the war expenditures committee was as effective as proved to be and I agree with the Prime Minister that it did very good work.
The war expenditures committee sat in camera; no one could get any advantage in publicity out of its discussions. The only way in which members of that committee could achieve any kind of reputation was by doing exactly what the committee was directed by the house to do, namely to seek

ways of saving the taxpayers' money, and that in a field in which, as the hon. member for Ottawa West has pointed out, there were no precise estimates at all a field where huge sums of money were voted which were spent by the government in whatever ways seemed most expedient for the prosecution of the war. There was a scope there that does not exist in the ordinary civil estimates. But I have no doubt that one of the reasons why this committee did concentrate on its primary function was the reason I have indicated.
I should like to join the hon. member for Ottawa West in the appeal he made to the Prime Minister. I certainly intend to vote for this motion, whether the Prime Minister listens to the appeal or not. The right hon. gentleman pointed out that the committee of supply-and he quoted some important authorities to support this view-was too large to consider the estimates in an orderly and effective manner. I agree with that, but it does seem to me that a committee of 60 would also be too large, and for two reasons, one of which is that the larger the committee the less a personal sense of responsibility may be felt by individual members. An hon. member is going to say: well, there are 60 of us. If I have something else to do, nobody is going to miss me, anyway.
I may be wrong, but it does seem to me that a committee of about half that size, indeed, a committee of the size we had in 1955, 1956 and the first part of 1957, would be very well suited for this task. When I was before that committee the attendance seemed good and the interest seemed to be reasonably well sustained, as Your Honour will perhaps recall. I have a feeling there would be both more orderly discussion and a greater sense of responsibility in the committee if it were smaller.
It may be that the government envisages the committee being divided into subcommittees which could work concurrently. That might to some degree invalidate the argument I am making. But I have a feeling it is going to be very difficult to get the kind of expert consideration which the Prime Minister indicated in his opening remarks he would like to see given to the estimates, if more than one department is before the committee at any particular time. However, that is a point on which there could be differing views. I do feel, though, that to attempt to have all 60 members of the committee, or a substantial majority of them, sitting at one time, would make it very difficult to have the kind of detailed and orderly discussion that we achieved when I was before the committee in 1955 and which, I have been told by others who appeared

later before that committee, was continued after the estimates of my former department had been dealt with.
Hon. members will recall that it was customary in those three years to change considerably the personnel of the estimates committee when a new department went before it, so to have a smaller committee would not mean restricting the number of members who could serve on the committee. I certainly would not wish the Prime Minister or any other member to feel I am suggesting that 60 people are not competent to serve on the committee, but I am suggesting that this is too large a number to have serving at one and the same time if we are to accomplish the purpose which I think both the government and the opposition would like to see this committee perform.
There is one other thing I should like to say, and again I am echoing the words of my leader, about the external affairs committee. I do think that setting up a committee on estimates and having departments come before it has been a very good thing for the departments. I think the mere act of preparing for the work of the committee had a very helpful effect on the civil service and upon the ministers, too. It is so easy-and we know this is true in our personal affairs and in every other way- to leave things as they are and not to change them if we do not have to defend them before someone else. And even though there was nothing wrong-and there rarely was anything wrong-there were often things that were redundant and unnecessary but which went on from year to year. But when it is incumbent on civil servants to explain why these things are being done, and upon ministers to defend the continued existence of such conditions, I believe it had a very salutary effect on the administration of a department. I should like to say that I am not expressing these views for the first time now that I am in opposition; I expressed them long before the committee on estimates was set up, and even before I was a member of this house.
It seems to me it would be a good idea to have a regular rotation of departments so that every three or four years each department would have been before the committee.
I believe we would get dividends from such a practice, not in money savings perhaps, but in better value for the money that is allocated.
I may say, in conclusion, that I am heartily in accord with the purpose of the motion.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members of the house will agree that this has been a very useful discussion. I am impressed again, however, by the attitude of clinging to the type of thinking which existed on this side
Additional Standing Committees of the house a year ago as exemplified by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and also by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate (Mr. Pickersgill) who has just resumed his seat.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: An attitude of responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
There is about his approach to this question this attitude of hopelessness and of stagnation which was so prevalent under the former administration and, which, I suggest, was one of the main reasons why there have been such drastic changes in the political life of Canada within the last 11 months.
Our approach to this question arises out of many long, weary years of being in opposition and trying to improve the functioning of parliamentary committees, and when it came to being a reactionary on questions of this type-questions having to do with the functioning of parliament-there certainly was no greater or more deeply dyed reactionary than the late Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: He was absolutely against any changes in the rules of the House of Commons. If I remember correctly, from the time I came to the house in 1935, until his retirement from public life, not one substantial change was made in the rules. And now we see his disciple, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, following the same reactionary line of thinking.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: Surely the hon. gentleman does not object to conservatism.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
This amendment is introduced in an attempt to increase the efficiency of the House of Commons, not only by setting up an estimates committee but also by setting up a committee on veterans affairs, which is equally important and about which so far so little has been said. This latter committee has been advocated by the great veterans organizations of this country for many years, advocated by all of the parties in opposition and yet for some reason or other the Liberal government would never make this move. They seemed to be afraid that if there were a standing committee on veterans affairs meeting every year a request might be made for improvements in veterans legislation with which they were not prepared to deal. At all times they resisted the setting up of a standing committee on veterans affairs. In fact, on different occasions when a special committee was set up during one session, the former government confined the powers of that special committee on veterans affairs to the legislation the government was
SS6	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Additional Standing Committees prepared to submit to the committee, so that there could be no general discussion whatever of the problems facing those Canadians who had been willing to sacrifice their lives for their fellow Canadians or the problems of the dependants of those who did make the great sacrifice. Now we are taking this step of setting up a standing committee on veterans affairs so that each year all the legislation for the benefit of veterans can be reviewed and kept up to date. My understanding is that the estimates of this department are to be referred to the standing committee, just as has been done with great success, as the Leader of the Opposition said this morning, in the case of the external affairs estimates.
As for the estimates committee, our motives for setting it up are perfectly straightforward and entirely sincere. We believe that it can be of great benefit to the House of Commons; that it will mean greater efficiency in the business of this chamber. By having the committee consider the estimates of certain departments we are not taking power away from the committee of supply, which is a committee of the whole house, not taking away from the house, the right to go into each and every one of those estimates, just as has been done with the estimates of the Department of External Affairs.
Hon. members who have been here for any length of time must agree that there is no opportunity in this house when estimates are under consideration to go carefully into the details of each vote. Sometimes half a dozen votes will go through without one word being said about them; particularly when the weather is hot and we are near the end of a session when we are sitting in the mornings and on Wednesday and Friday evenings and on Saturdays there is a great tendency to let votes slip through.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: That happens in committees, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: It was in a Liberal committee that that happened. We are going to have a new type of activity in the committee. The Leader of the Opposition, like the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, has been on the government side too long; he has got stale, just like the other members of the former Liberal government. I agree that if the vast majority of members on those committees were supporters of the former government a great many things would be passed by and a good many other things would be covered up. We are not like that.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend misunderstood. I said things were allowed to slip through in committee by the opposition members on those committees at that time for the reasons he indicated.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Well, the opposition members on those committees under the former government certainly did not have very much help from any Liberal members in dealing with the business before those committees. It is a new era, Mr. Speaker. These hon. members do not seem to realize that we are living in new days in Canada. There is hope in this land once more; there is a new and far broader and finer vision than there was when he was in power.
I was somewhat surprised by the attitude of the leader of the C.C.F., the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), this morning who, in referring to the new members who happen to be supporters of the government, indicated that he was very much afraid that the only reason those committees are being set up is to keep those new members out of mischief.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: And the hon. member for Ottawa West says, "hear, hear!" He is still back in the bygone age as well. He is thinking of the time when they had about 150 or 160 trained seals over here-

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: Look at them flap now.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: Seals in training.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: -on the Liberal side of the house, as it was at that time.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit a question? Is the purpose of the committee to find mischief for the new members to do?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: I thought the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was a little more enlightened in his attitude toward this question than the hon. member for Assiniboia. Apparently, he is in the same deep rut. Naturally, one way of making this house more efficient is to give every private member, no matter to which party he may belong, the greatest possible scope in taking part in the government of the country. This is something that should have been done by the former government and why they were not bright enough to see the need for it I never could understand.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: Are you not glad they were not?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
I am very glad they were not. That is one reason why they got such a defeat on June 10 of last year and March 31 of this year. They were just too smug and
self-centred to see the need of some step of this kind.
We have in this house more than 150 members who have not been members for a year.

Of course, the vast majority of them are supporters of the present government.
These men come here representing hundreds of thousands of constituents across this country. They come here with their ideas of what they can do to help their fellow Canadians and to improve government in Canada. There has never been such an influx of new members at one time in the history of this nation, and I think the hon. member for Assiniboia was being very unfair and unwise-mind you, it is a very rare occasion when I would accuse him of either of these attitudes-in sneering at the new members and saying that these committees are only going to be set up in order to give them something to do, to keep them out of mischief.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: He has a lot to learn himself yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
We believe that the new members, no matter on what side of the house they sit, can make a tremendous contribution to Canada during the next four years and we propose to give them every possible opportunity to do so.
Some hon. members have asked questions about the estimates committee. For example, they ask who will decide what estimates are to be studied by the committee. We believe that the committee itself should be free to decide what departmental estimates it wishes to consider. Mind you, we will be ready to move that the estimates of the Department of National Defence be referred to that committee for the reason that they are very large and involve more money than the estimates of any other department. They are set up in a general way and are not broken down into many small items as is the case with the Department of Transport. As the national defence estimates have never been before the estimates committee in the past, it does seem that it would be common sense to give the estimates committee an opportunity to go over them. That, of course, would probably mean going over the estimates of the Department of Defence Production which is the procurement agency for the Department of National Defence and actually spends quite a large proportion of the defence department vote. In addition, of course, the Department of Defence Production has under its jurisdiction five different crown companies and a study of the work of these crown companies would be intensely interesting.
There is no reason why the work of the estimates committee should be restricted to the estimates of these two departments. We would hope there would be time for them to consider the estimates of some of the other departments.
Additional Standing Committees

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question before he leaves that particular subject? Is it contemplated, for instance, that when the estimates of the Department of National Defence are up for consideration by the committee the chiefs of staff and serving officers responsible to the Canadian government will be called before that committee to be examined?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
I am not in a position to say that. That would have to be decided at the time. We believe that members of all parties will be trying to do a job on the estimates committee and we do not expect that they will be unreasonable even though they happen to be sitting on the other side of the house.
Some members also asked whether the committees, I presume not only these two but all committees functioning this year, would be sitting while the house is sitting. There again common sense will have to prevail. We have had occasion to complain in the past about being dragged out of the house to committees all over the parliament buildings when we should have been in the house. Sometimes we did not get very much consideration from the Liberal government. We are planning to be so much better than the Liberal government in this and many other respects.
Then there was some question about committee chairmen. The chairman of a committee of the house is quite an important person. He has very wide powers and we do not intend that those powers shall be confined. This is one reason we wonder why Liberal members are so coy about the suggestion that one of their members should be chairman of the public accounts committee.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: It should not have been in the throne speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
They back away from it and seem to suspect that here is a Trojan horse. They are not quite sure what is inside it and seem to think that probably it may hold a lot of Tories ready to jump out and bite them. But I point out that the chairman of a committee has extensive powers.
The hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) asked whether the house would be required to concur in all reports of committees.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: The method of reporting of the estimates committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
There again it is impossible to foretell the best way to deal with this situation. There may be many committee reports which do not require concurrence. As he himself knows, when a report is

Additional Standing Committees brought in which is unanimous and is not controversial there is no need to have concurrence moved in the house. If I remember correctly, the practice of his own government was to move concurrence very rarely if there was going to be any debate about the matter. I do not remember any occasion when the Liberal government provided for a debate where there was a real dispute in a committee. There may have been one or two but certainly there were not many.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question on this point? The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) indicated that one of the purposes of the committee, and I rather think he indicated it as the main purpose, was to attempt to effect economies. I was wondering how the minister envisaged the mechanics of that. Would the committee itself move that an item in the estimates be reduced or would it merely make a report saying that the government should give consideration to reducing the item?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member is a very good one to bring up this question.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: It is purely a mechanical question.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: While many members would try to make suggestions to bring about economies, I remember how hard he pressed me during the whole of the last session to build him a post office at Wesleyville.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: It will not be the last pressure either.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: To get a post office built at Wesleyville seemed to be his main concern throughout the whole of the last session. We have actually got it under construction and I thought I would be through with him for the next few years.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: You are sadly mistaken.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: I am confident that the suggestions made in this committee will lead to economies. In the departments with which I have had short experience-

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: I do not think the minister understood my question. It was not whether or not there would be economies; it was just the mechanical way of dealing with them. Did the minister envisage the committee moving to reduce an item or did he envisage them simply making a report that the government should give consideration to the possibility of reducing an item?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
I would think the committee could only make a report. The committee


of itself would not have the power to reduce items because that jurisdiction remains in the committee of supply.
Then some mention was made of the size of the estimates committee, and here there is certainly room for disagreement. All of these steps that are taken are not, of necessity, the last and final steps. We hope that we are much more ready to make changes than was the former government. If it should be found that the plan does not work out well, then changes could be made. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate came very near the point when he suggested that it might happen there would be some subcommittees set up under the estimates committee. Of course, if there were 60 members on the committee it would be possible to do that. These questions can be looked at in the light of the experience the committee itself has in the days ahead.
I should like to say a word or two about the intention with regard to sending estimates to other committees. The practice has been to send only the estimates of the Department of External Affairs to a standing committee. The Leader of the Opposition knows that practice has not been in existence for very long. We agree with him that the work of that committee has been very worth-while, and part of the credit for that success must go to the Leader of the Opposition for the way in which he, his deputy minister and his officials have carried on before that committee. I was a member of the first committee on external affairs and served for several years. It was very informative and interesting work. We see no reason why the same kind of success cannot be achieved by other standing committees, for example the standing committee on veterans affairs. If the house is willing we are considering also, for example, that the fisheries estimates might be referred to the standing committee on marine and fisheries; that the estimates of the Department of Mines and Techincal Surveys and perhaps northern affairs and national resources, might be referred to the standing committee on mines, forests and waters. This standing committee has never met during the whole 22 years I have been a member of parliament and yet mining problems, forestry, conservation and northern development have become of tremendous importance to Canada. They could have been considered by this committee.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Would the minister permit a question at that point? In sending the estimates to the estimates committee it is quite obvious that the terms of reference would be very restrictive, namely an attempt to secure economies. If estimates were sent

to functional committees, would those committees really be transformed into estimates committees for that purpose or would they be considering the policies of the departments? There is a question of principle there that I think is very important to our whole parliamentary system.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: I come back to the standing committee on external affairs. I think it could not be described as a committee which was only meeting to effect economies. It is designed to have a look at the whole of the Department of External Affairs.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: It is a policy committee, in other words.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
It is not a policy committee in the sense that it lays down policy, but it does have a chance to go into the activities of the external affairs department. I am trying to be quite frank about our approach to the question, and we are merely trying to increase the efficiency of the House of Commons.
Then, the estimates of the Department of Labour might be referred to the standing committee on industrial relations. We are not insistent on this course being followed, but we do hold it out to the members of the opposition parties for consideration, and do suggest to them that if steps of this kind are taken they will probably greatly increase the efficiency of the house and will give far more members of the house an opportunity to take a very effective part in the business of the house.
We must keep a certain number of departmental estimates available for consideration in the house. We cannot refer them all to committees or we might run out of business in the house. Here again, if one is practical and uses common sense, it is necessary that some of the estimates be reserved for consideration here at any time.
This is just a general summary of the situation as we see it. We appreciate the fact that members of the official opposition and of the C.C.F. are supporting this motion. We suggest that if everybody enters into the work which will be sent to these committees there will be a great service rendered to the country and the House of Commons will be a great deal more efficient than it has been.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question before he sits down? He has been very patient and very helpful. Could he inform the house whether it is the intention to operate the committee on public accounts in accordance with the British practice governing that committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
The public accounts committee is not the type of committee to which you
Additional Standing Committees could send estimates. It merely deals with the accounts for the previous years. I am not in a position to say just what course will be followed in the public accounts committee and that, too, will have to be worked out on a reasonable basis. I realize that the public accounts committee in the past has sometimes been a bit of a political bear-garden-again, under a Liberal regime.
I recall being a member of the public accounts committee-

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) does not look too happy at that observation.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: I am not talking about the war expenditures committee, I am talking about the public accounts committee. There is a very big difference. I recall being a member of the public accounts committee, just before the second war, when we investigated the Bren gun deal, when there were no holds barred. We kept on sitting until parliament was dissolved over in the Senate.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is not offering that to the new members as an example of how to behave in parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: I am offering that as an example of how a Liberal government behaves.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am always reluctant to take up the time of the house, but I rise in this occasion to further express our support of this motion and to make one or two very brief observations. First, I should like to correct an apparent misunderstanding on the part of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) of some remarks made by our leader this morning. If I heard the minister correctly, and he always tried to be quite fair, he accused the leader of this group of sneering somewhat about the number of members the government proposed to put on this committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: I accused the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) of sneering at the new members, and saying probably one of the main reasons these committees were to be set up this year was to keep the new members out of mischief.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
I just want to explain the point made by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). He was simply saying it was reported in the press to that effect. There were others who implied that the government were not as lily-white as it was presumed to be on the surface. I might say that it is not our intention in this group to sneer. We always aim to steer.
As one who has been a member of a good many committees during my tenure in this
700	HOUSE OF
Additional Standing Committees house over the last 13 years I am personally pleased to see this resolution introduced. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that when members on the government side of the house were in opposition, year after year we with them repeatedly asked for standing committees on estimates and veterans affairs. Personally, I am glad that the government is taking this action and has responded to those pleas that have been made throughout the years. This fact gives me considerable pleasure and satisfaction.
In addition to that, I am quite sure that there will be other people outside this house who will be pleased to know of the appointment of these committees not only on the part of those who are interested in administration and expenditures in general but on the part of those interested in veterans affairs. I am quite sure the Canadian Legion, the national council of veterans, veterans and their dependants and all persons interested in the welfare of veterans will be pleased to know there is to be a standing committee on veterans affairs to give, I hope, an annual review to the problems that arise in connection with legislation. While the special committees on these subjects have done excellent work in years past, it is obvious that in a changing and increasingly complex society it is necessary to give much closer and, shall I say, continuing attention to much of this legislation than was the habit in years past. I think the government has responded correctly to the changing situations and circumstances.
The minister made a reference to the standing committee on mines, forests and waters which has not sat, according to his knowledge, for the last 21 years or 22 years. I know it has not sat during my 13 years here. From that reference one could possibly infer that, although we had standing committees, they did not necessarily function every session; that they may be appointed but may not be called together to do any work. As far as estimates are concerned, I am quite sure that there are enough members on this side and on all sides who are sufficiently interested in administration and expenditures to make certain that any government calls that committee to meet annually. So far as veterans affairs are concerned, I am quite certain that the veterans organizations will make certain that they have the opportunity to present their views and to bring evidence to the attention of the standing committee annually.
Before concluding my brief remarks I want to refer to the attitude of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill)-I must be careful with that name-on two points. He first of all criticized the number on the committee and, if 

I heard him correctly, suggested that a smaller number of members of parliament on a committee would be more responsible than a larger number of members of parliament on a committee. I thought that was rather a reflection upon the sense of responsibility of members of parliament and, I should think, rather a reflection on the developing processes of democracy. I think we should always be trying to inform more and more people all the time. In addition to that, I am all for a good sized committee for practical and other reasons.
First of all, we all know that it is not possible for all members of the committee to attend every meeting of it. I am all in favour of as large a number of members of this house as possible and practical having the opportunity to hear the officials of various departments, learn of the administration of the departments, make inquiries and so on, so that they are better informed as a result of being members of that committee. For that reason I am personally glad that the one committee has 60 members on it and that the other has 40 members.
The other remark made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was to the effect that he fears abuse of the committee, something after the manner of what he considers is the abuse of committees in the United States, if I heard him correctly, in that there would be too many organizations coming before them or too much evidence presented.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: I am afraid the hon. member did not hear me correctly. What I said was that it seemed to me that the estimates committee would have enough to do to examine the officials, that that should be its prime object, and that I could not see much purpose to be served by having outside witnesses in the estimates committee.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: I ask the hon. member to excuse me, then. The hon. member was referring to the estimates committee only?

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: Yes; the estimates committee only.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: I understood him at the time to be speaking of both committees.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
I should like to say that in my opinion it would be most unwise to deny the peoples' organizations representing any strata in society the opportunity to come before an estimates committee if occasion arises. I would not favour an overdevelopment or abuse of that sort of thing but I think it is something that should be permitted and allowed if it serves the public good and is to the public advantage.

With these tew remarks I propose to sit down. But before doing so I again want to say that we in this group are highly pleased at the introduction of this amendment and the opportunity which it presents for the improvement of increasing numbers of members of this house in their knowledge of parliamentary affairs and government administration.
Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker,-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: I must inform the house that if the Prime Minister speaks now he will [DOT]close the debate.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
-I am not going to retrace the steps that have already been taken. In general I think that this has been a very good debate and one in which members participating have shown a realization of the purpose the government has in mind in placing this resolution before the house, namely the improvement of the processes of parliament.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) referred to the system in the United States and I could not be more in agreement with him than I am. I would not want to see an extension of our committee system to the end that the one in effect in the congress of the United States would be appended to our system. It is quite impossible to give to committees here the same responsibilities as those that are accorded to committees in congress for, as was pointed out so clearly by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), under our system of government the executive has responsibilities that cannot be delegated, abdicated or indeed abrogated in any way. The hope was expressed by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that the committee when set up should not be subject to television. I know this house would not be the same without him here. I say that with great respect. I am sure that he is no more desirous than are any of the rest of us to have a projection of any instrument or institution of government through the medium of television or radio.
In speaking of my hon. friend, may I say that I always listen to him with great interest. He has a way of describing the operations of democracy that gives full regard to his academic days and reveals his knowledge of history. In addition he has something that most of us do not have. He has the knowledge and the viewpoint of the civil servant. I am sure during the days when he served while under the distinguished tutelage of one of the masters of constitutional development in our [DOT]country, the late Mr. King, the hon. member
Additional Standing Committees for Bonavista-Twillingate did have more than a platonic interest in the political implications of these matters.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: I did my duty.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: Yes, I do not doubt that you did. Having said that, I wish to make one or two references to what the Leader of the Opposition said today, and with that I will conclude. Apparently his viewpoint-the hon. gentleman also having a background of experience in the civil service-caused him to state that this committee was too large with 60 as its personnel. He suggested that it would not operate as effectively as it would if it had a smaller personnel. As has just been pointed out by the hon. gentleman who preceded me, the statement made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was to the effect that the larger the committee, the lesser the sense of responsibility. I was quite interested in that remark. The Leader of the Opposition pointed out that the public accounts committee in the United Kingdom was composed of 15 members and apparently in smallness there is strength.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: We seek what consolation we can find.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
I thought I would scan the composition of various committees of this house as constituted under the government that was in power for 22 years to ascertain whether the ideas we have heard advanced today were the same as the views held by members of that government in days gone by. I find that the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines for years has been composed of 60 members. The committee on agriculture and colonization has had 60 members. The committee on miscellaneous private bills, the banking and commerce committee and the public accounts committee have had 50 members each. The other committees, one or two of which have not met for years, have lesser numbers of personnel.
As far as I am concerned there is nothing particularly binding about the size of this committee but I felt it should be large enough to permit it to appoint subcommittees in respect of particular subjects if it so desired in its attempt to discharge the responsibility referred to by the Leader of the Opposition of giving acute examination to those matters referred to it.
While my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition was speaking I thought I would examine the records of the past to find out whether or not the proposal we have now placed before the house ever received support from hon. gentlemen of the same political persuasion of those sitting opposite. On page

Additional Standing Committees 956 of Hansard of February 8, 1955, in some remarks I made at that time on the subject of the special committee on estimates, I find reference to the fact that in 1921 the late Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux brought before the house a resolution in these words:
That, in the opinion of this house, in order to co-ordinate and expedite the business of parliament in a more intelligent and practical way, the estimates of the various departments should, before being laid on the table, be scrutinized by a special committee of the house, where officers would be summoned to appear with plans and reports bearing on each appropriation.
Among those who participated in the debate was the then leader of the opposition, Mr. Mackenzie King.
My hon. friend asked, is there something revolutionary about this? There is nothing revolutionary about it because it has been suggested on a number of occasions in recent years by those of us who today sit on this side of the house. It is interesting to observe the reactions of my hon. friends to the recommendations we are now bringing into effect, for after all the things we advocated in opposition in order to improve, raise and augment the sense of responsibility and the opportunity of service of parliament are today being implemented at the first opportunity. On February 28, 1956 the motion made by the then prime minister was in these words, as reported at page 1639 of Hansard of that date:
That a select committee to be designated be appointed to consider such of the estimates as may be referred to it and to report from time to time its findings and recommendations to the house.
On that same date it was moved by the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), the then private member for Kamloops, as reported at page 1641 of Hansard:
That the motion be amended by adding thereto the following words:
"and that the said committee have power to send for persons, papers and records".
These are almost the very same words to which Mr. King had given support earlier. It is interesting to look at the vote on this amendment to the motion which occurred on February 28. I find that my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition and also the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) were among those who voted against giving the committee the right to bring before it persons, papers and records.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the Prime Minister would tell the house what committee was under discussion at that time?

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS TO SET UP ADDITIONAL COMMITTEES
speechtext:
The estimates committee, the one we are dealing with now, and that is what surprised me. I am not in a provocative mood today at all, nor am I in that state


of mind, after the high level on which this debate has continued, but I am glad to see that the shades of opposition have had an effect on my hon. friends and that the things they were opposed to then they are prepared to support today.
One thing which was made extremely clear by the Leader of the Opposition was that to the maximum extent there should be no interference with the business of the house by the sittings of the committee and I could not be more in agreement with that, because we do not want the sittings of the committee to supplant in any way the operations of the House of Commons whether in formal debate or otherwise.
Someone mentioned that we should not endeavour to rush parliament. In other words, every opportunity should be given for the fullest consideration of the matters that come before the house, and that is true. Our system of parliament is based on the maintenance and assurance of the two party system. I am not speaking of the changes that have taken place in any critical sense at all, but there is no doubt but that one of the reasons parliament has been extended on and on in its sittings has been due to a multiplicity of parties with each party endeavouring to have its say. The repetition has added nothing to clarification of the issues and the debate of them. I would be the last to want to press hon. gentlemen opposite in any way to withdraw any of their rights of debate, and I give them that assurance. That is one of the major objectives I have in mind.
I realize, as I mentioned on an earlier occasion, that someone will say that with the very large majority of the government the rights of minorities might be in jeopardy. I want not only to assure but to reassure both this house and the country as a whole that such a viewpoint does not, and will not, merit the support of members of this government. We wish to make this House of Commons as efficient and as effective as it is possible to do. Normally the estimates take about 20 days in a five month session. It is interesting to note in this connection that in the United Kingdom the period for the discussion of estimates is restricted to 20 days. Throughout the years we have found it to be the case that certain estimates appear periodically and continue more or less throughout the entire period of the session. It is not the purpose in setting up this committee to deny to any hon. member, including the members of the committee, their right to debate fully any item that has been dealt with by the committee when the estimates are returned to this chamber. But I have found, as has the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate

with that dual experience he has had as a civil servant and a minister of the crown, and also I may say, as a most observant political philosopher, that the consideration of items in the committee and the information elicited there does achieve a reduction in the time spent on debate in this chamber. After all, much of the information which has been obtained can then be placed before the committee of the whole in summary form.
I will simply conclude by thanking the hon. gentlemen who have participated in this debate for their contributions. As far as the composition of committees is concerned, provision has been made both by tradition and otherwise as to the proportions of the membership of standing committees and the like. It would, naturally, be difficult for any group with a small membership to have hon. members actively associated in the work of all the committees. But I do say-and I speak particularly to the members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition-that our purpose will be to assure to the greatest degree possible, consistent with the achievement of a businesslike examination of the estimates, that those things that can be done in order to ease the load that rests on the private members in a committee who are also desirous of participating in the debates in the house will receive most serious consideration. This is one of the steps we are taking. There are going to be further steps which will be revealed in due course under that general heading in the speech from the throne "Improving and enlarging the opportunities for service in the parliament of our country."
Mention was made of research assistance. I am not going to discuss that at this time. That is just one of the facets of this question. Over the years when we were in opposition we suggested that something of this sort might be brought about. We are now taking preliminary steps toward the improvement of the mechanics for the achievement of reasonable and reasoned consideration of the problems which face us.
We welcome the suggestions we received today, given, as they were, in a spirit of co-operation. We will in the days ahead endeavour to enlarge the field of experiment, if you will, based on the experience of the past, so that parliament may be able to discharge its responsibilities with that sense of urgency which the situation demands. Again, I thank hon. gentlemen opposite for the contributions they have made. It is, indeed, a happy thing to see uniformity of support for a proposition which we on this side of the house advocated in opposition.

Motion agreed to.

that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act to authorize contributions being made as of the first day of July, 1958, to a participating province which has a plan in operation; and to make certain changes in connection with the administration of the act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sevigny in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the
basic purport of this resolution is to give effect to the announcement which I made to the house during the last parliament on January 10, 1958. It is, I believe, self-explanatory and I will therefore postpone any statement until after the bill has been introduced. I should point out that the latter part of the resolution suggesting certain changes in connection with the administration of the act has to do with very minor adjustments and amendments which are being put forward at the suggestion of the provincial governments. They clarify generally accepted views as to drugs and meals for in-patients and out-patients.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Does the minister not intend to make a further statement.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I have a statement prepared, Mr. Chairman. I think it would be more acceptable at second reading stage.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I would think, Mr. Chairman, if I may say so with a desire to assist the minister, that in a matter as important as this, and in view of the fact that this is the first opportunity the administration has had to report on a subject of such great interest, the minister might find it more convenient to make that statement now. When it comes to the bill we will go into its details, but we should now have a comprehensive statement from the minister. What the minister has said thus far does not give us very much indication of what progress has been made in this important matter, and what amendments, other than the provision for the date of federal payments, are being provided. I would suggest that my hon. friend might find it helpful all around if he took the course suggested.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
If I may add a word at this time, I think it has been normal practice for a minister, in introducing a major resolution such as this one, to give the committee at least the advantage of a brief outline of the main points the government has in mind

Hospital Insurance Act and the main parts of the bill. It is true that an explanation was made in a previous session but that was in a previous parliament. In view of the fact that this is the time when we discuss the whole general question before a bill is introduced, I think the minister will agree, from his own experience in this house, that very often the administration makes a number of changes because of the discussion. I do not see how we can intelligently discuss what the government's intention may be if we do not have the benefit of a statement at this time.
I do not wish my remarks to be taken in any critical way. I believe the government is carrying on negotiations with a number of provinces. From what little knowledge I have, at least in some regard real progress is being made; but surely when such an important question as this is being discussed hon. members should have the initial advantage of a statement from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I have no objection to giving a statement now. I had thought that possibly it would be more convenient to have the bill before us to discuss the clauses which I am proposing to be amended. However, I will say a few words at this time.
It is the government's intention to introduce an amendment to the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act at this stage, as reported in the resolution and as set forth in the announcement of January 10 last. At that time I explained that we propose to repeal section 6(2) of the act and to replace section 6(2) with a new section authorizing the dominion government to make contributions as of July 1, 1958 to any provinces which had signed an agreement and which had a provincial law in force.
When the bill is before the house hon. members of the committee will see that the government is seeking at this stage to carry out this commitment to the people of Canada. We are also proposing two relatively minor changes in section 2 of the act dealing with certain services which are provided thereunder. Section 6(2) in its present form reads:
No contributions shall be paid under this act until at least six provinces, containing at least one-hall the population of Canada, have entered into an agreement, and the provincial law in relation to those provinces is in force.
This clause could prohibit federal financial participation in provincial hospital insurance schemes until at least one of Canada's two central provinces is prepared to put an insurance program into operation. Of these key provinces, only Ontario has agreed to participate, and as of January 1, 1959. The result of this provision as it now stands

could be to postpone the whole undertaking until the first of next year. We came to the conclusion some time ago that such a delay was unnecessary, and indeed undesirable, in view of the fact that a number of provinces indicated that their schemes could be ready well in advance of January, 1959. Because it was obvious that there would not be time to introduce a formal amendment to the act during the last session of parliament and because it was important for the provinces to know our intentions in preparing their budgets for the current fiscal year, the government last January did give notice of its plans in this respect.
In my announcement last January I expressed the hope that at least three or four provinces would try to have their programs ready by July 1. It now appears that I was somewhat pessimistic, since five provinces, British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Newfoundland have indicated their desire to begin operations by July 1. These provinces have been working very closely with the officials of my own and other federal departments which are interested in the matter. Similar consultations have been held and are going forward with other provinces having target dates set for 1959. In addition to Ontario, which has already signed an agreement with the dominion government, two provinces, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, hope to commence operations on January 1 next.
While agreeing to participate in the program, Prince Edward Island has not yet indicated the date on which it will be prepared to proceed.
The degree of co-operation which has developed between the two senior levels of government in connection with the program has been very encouraging. In the past months I have had a series of meetings and discussions with provincial ministers, all of whom have show a whole-hearted willingness to work together in bringing this project to reality at the earliest possible date.
The officials of my department have made trips to provincial capitals and we in turn have had provincial delegations visit us here in Ottawa. In addition, there have been two technical conferences attended by representatives of all the provinces. Throughout there has been an excellent spirit of team work exhibited on all sides which to my mind holds great promise for the program's future success.
The amendment which I have just mentioned in section 6(2) is the major proposal. However, in this resolution we are also proposing to change section 2(f) (iv) which simply clarifies the already generally accepted view to the effect that drugs, biologicals and

related preparations, as specified in the agreement, may be considered as insured services only when actually administered in hospital. In other words, these items will not be covered under the program on a take-home basis.
As for the amendment to section 2(i), this deletes the present exclusion of drugs, accommodation and meals which provincial schemes may provide to outpatients. In detailed discussions with regard to this portion of the act, it is generally agreed that drugs form an essential part of out-patient treatment and should therefore be included among the insure items which provinces may select in this connection. Again, however, they would be for use in hospital only and will not be available on a take-home basis.
With respect to the provision of meals and accommodation to out-patients, it is considered that this would tend to deter admission to hospitals under certain circumstances and thus to reduce the demand for inpatient services.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that covers the intent behind the resolution and I would be glad to hear from the other members of the committee and answer any questions, if I am able to.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I thank the minister for giving us at least this preview of the amendments. I must say I am a little disappointed that the minister was not in a position, or did not at this time see fit to give us a more comprehensive review of the state of the negotiations that were authorized under the measure which was passed by parliament in the month of March, 1957 and before the election which was held on June 10 of that year.
Hon. members know the amendment my hon. friend is proposing is based upon the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, the resolution for which was presented to parliament by the previous administration on March 25, 1957; a measure which won wide approval in the house notwithstanding certain criticisms of it from some quarters; a measure that represents a very considerable assumption of financial responsibility by the government of Canada on behalf of the taxpayers of the country; a measure which now makes possible on a nationwide basis, if sufficient provinces enter into the arrangement, a scheme of hospital insurance and diagnostic services.
I want to thank the hon. member for Durham, who in his observations in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, so generously referred to the leadership in this matter by the government 57071-3-45
Hospital Insurance Act headed by Mr. St. Laurent and for his generous references to my participation in the promotion of hospital insurance. I thank him very much and I am sorry he is not here to hear me in this expression of thanks to him. May I in turn say to the hon. member for Durham that when I was minister of national health and welfare I greatly appreciated the collaboration received from him as a member of the staff of McGill University medical school, notably in connection with the establishment of the cancer institute.
I think it is important that we should bear in mind the reason why this particular amendment is now found necessary. Under the act as it now stands section 6, subsection 2, provides:
No contributions shall be paid under this act until at least six provinces, containing at least one-hall the population of Canada, have entered into an agreement, and the provincial law in relation to those provinces is in force.
It will be remembered that when that section was introduced some hon. gentlemen criticized it on the grounds that the federal government should pay out moneys at once to those provinces which had schemes of hospital insurance in operation. I indicated at that time that the reason for this particular clause was that we wanted to develop a nationwide scheme of hospital insurance in Canada and that if we wanted to give expression in the form of financial assistance to those provinces that had schemes in operation we should have done so a long time ago. I pointed out that what we were after then was to get other provinces where there were no hospital insurance programs to the point where they would agree to share with the federal government in a hospital and diagnostic services' scheme. I am sure that events have more than justified the course which the government of that day pursued.
If we had not insisted on having at least six provinces we would not now be in the position which the minister is now in being able to report on the extent to which progress even on an apparently limited basis has been made. But the minister will remember that last fall I asked him and the government of the day to give us an explanation as to why no agreements had been signed between any of the provinces and the federal government. The situation was that the present act came into being just prior to the election in 1957 and understandably there was no opportunity during that event for negotiations between the then federal government and the provinces, although during the course of the election campaign the province of Prince Edward Island did indicate its willingness to come into the scheme, making that province the sixth

Hospital Insurance Act to come within the ambit of subsection 2 of section 6 of the present act.
But from the time the present administration took office until this very day we have not had any substantial report in the house indicating the extent to which the government has succeeded in its negotiations with the provinces. As of last October there were three provinces with schemes in being, the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan. I inquired last fall and I inquire now why no agreements have been signed with these provinces or am I to assume that agreements have been signed with them? I know that an agreement was signed with the province of Ontario during the middle of the last general election campaign. I do not blame my hon. friend for taking advantage of that particular moment to conclude such an agreement. I was glad to see an agreement had been signed with Ontario. I had hoped that it would have been possible to sign an agreement with Ontario, the senior and largest province, long before March of this year. I am sure, as I indicated last fall, that an agreement could have been signed with the province of Ontario not later than the end of September of 1957.
But happy as one may be with the signature of the province of Ontario, what has happened to the agreements with the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan? Why have no agreements been signed with these provinces? Before we went out of office a master agreement was provided to each province that had indicated its willingness and interest and I had indicated to Premier Frost, who criticized this very provision, subsection 2 of section 6, that if by the end of September, 1957 we did not have six provinces in order to comply with this subsection we would, in view of the fact that Ontario was to begin its scheme on January 1, 1959, certainly take steps to modify the existing provision. That was an obvious assurance that had to be given. Otherwise we would have placed the province of Ontario in the very difficult position of starting its hospital insurance scheme on January 1, 1959 and not being able to count on the necessary contribution of the federal government amounting, speaking now from memory, to $60 million or 70 million a year. So I say I cannot understand why no agreements have been concluded with the other provinces and particularly the three provinces that now have schemes in existence.
The minister has indicated today that there is a fourth participating western province, the province of Manitoba. That is welcome news. We were all aware, of course, that for some time Manitoba has been seeking to get concessions from the federal government

which would make it possible for that province to enter into the arrangement. I hope the minister will tell us at some time what particular arrangements have been made with Manitoba.
I hope he will be able to tell us, for instance, whether or not it is true that Alberta is still not satisfied with the financial arrangements. Is it true that Alberta attended a conference here some few weeks ago and the delegates returned to that province without getting the kind of answers or the kind of satisfaction to which they felt they were entitled? I am not saying whether or not Alberta was right. I do not know what the argument was about, but I read a report in the newspapers that Alberta did leave here without any final arrangements being made with the federal government.
The minister has indicated to us that there are only two amendments before the house, one to provide for payments to any province, under certain conditions which will be outlined in the bill, by July 1 of this year. The other amendment is to provide for certain administrative changes which, as I understand, really make clear what was previously intended. These are the only two amendments that the minister proposes to bring before the house at this time. Certainly, so far as the amendment dealing with payments is concerned, there will be no opposition on our part. I suspect there will be no difficulty with regard to the other amendment, but I would prefer to see the actual wording, as would other hon. members, before giving any commitment in that particular.
It is important, having in mind the attitude taken by hon. gentlemen opposite when this measure was introduced, to remind them that the amendments they are making now do not represent to any degree the kind of amendments that they proposed when they were sitting on this side of the house or to amendments that were discussed in the federal election of 1957 and in the election held within the course of the last few months. The argument made against this measure by the present government when in opposition-I do not say by the present minister because he did not take part in those discussions so far as I can recollect-was that the bill was deficient in a number of particulars. First, the federal government was not assuming any responsibility for costs administration, nor was it assuming any responsibility for depreciation; it had excluded tuberculosis and mental illness as insurable items. Those four points represented the main criticisms of the opposition of that day, towards the hospital insurance bill which I had the responsibility of introducing.
We pointed out with regard to depreciation and cost of administration that those were

matters which we felt it was not fair to impose on the federal government in view of the very generous financial contribution it was then proposing to make to the provinces. It was pointed out also that the provinces then had not asked the federal government to bear these particular charges. Nevertheless, the present Minister of Justice and the former member for Lanark, at that time opposition critic in health and welfare matters, and others, criticized the government for not including depreciation and for not bearing a share of the cost of administration. These two items were discussed in the election of 1957. We were charged, in my own constituency with being callous to certain kinds of hospitals because we would not include federal responsibility for depreciation.
Then, with regard to tuberculosis and mental illness, an amendment was moved by the present Minister of Finance providing that tuberculosis and mental illness should be made insurable items under the bill. In answer to that argument of the present Minister of Finance, which was supported by the present Prime Minister, by the former member for Lanark and many other hon. members, we said that the bill was designed to assist individuals in their hospital costs and was not a measure designed to subsidize the provinces in any way. Since tuberculosis and mental illness were substantially taken care of in all provinces in provincial institutions at provincial cost it was illogical and unfair to argue that the federal government, under the hospital insurance scheme, should include those particular items. I pointed out, too, that in those provinces where they had hospital insurance, such as British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan, tuberculosis and mental illness were treated as separate items under separate accounts, altogether apart from hospital insurance.
The government pointed out also that in so far as any individual having to personally pay the cost of treatment for tuberculosis or mental illness in a non-provincial institution was concerned, that particular phase of the cost would be covered by the bill. I urged hon. members not to argue that discrimination was being made in the case of one illness as opposed to another. Nowithstanding this the present Minister of Finance, of all persons, moved by way of amendment, and his remarks will be found at page 3380 of Hansard for April 10, 1957, that the bill should include tuberculosis and mental illness. He made a very strong speech urging that the bill was deficient because tuberculosis and mental illness were not included. Then, the present Prime Minister, speaking at page 3386 of Hansard for the same date, said that the bill was deficient and that there 57071-3-45i
Hospital Insurance Act was discrimination being made against tuberculosis and mental illness. He talked that way during the two elections, notwithstanding the fact that his argument was not valid. The argument was not valid because tuberculosis and mental illness are now taken care of in provincial institutions and at provincial cost for the most part.
I indicated we were prepared to include tuberculosis and mental illness in so far as the individual had to meet the cost of these illnesses in psychiatric wings of general hospitals or in non-provincial tuberculosis centres or hospitals. Notwithstanding these facts, another amendment in different form was moved and supported by those who were in opposition at that time. This was another parliamentary device adopted to achieve the same end.
Now, having taken that position, and having urged it on the administration of the day, the minister will not misunderstand me if I do express some surprise at this time that the present government now offers only the two amendments. Having taken this strong position with regard to depreciation, the sharing of the cost of administration, the inclusion of tuberculosis and mental illness, hon. gentleman I am sure will not misunderstand my surprise because they have not incorporated these matters in the bill they now put forward.
I do not want anyone to argue from what I am saying now that what we did was not valid. I do not recede one iota from the position we took. I think the position we took was correct. I think the position my hon. friend is taking now is correct. This is a measure designed to assist individuals in their hospital care and not to subsidize the provinces. What I am saying is that my hon. friends, having taken the strong position that they did, a position which the Canadian people had a right to assume during the elections would result in changes, should now do more than bring forward two amendments to this hospital insurance act.
