The minister, of course, would be the first to deny the desirability of that situation. I would have thought that was likely the reason why it is now proposed that these payments be made as of July 1.
I want to say this with some reservations until I hear the full explanation from the minister, but my impression all along has been that there has been a great deal of delay since this government came into being in implementing this hospital insurance act. I feel that it will be difficult to satisfy the house as to why agreements could not have been concluded long before now with other provinces. I find it difficult to understand why an agreement was concluded with the province of Ontario only about two months ago. In any event, these are some of the questions with which I hope the minister will deal before we come to the bill itself.
My hon. friend says that five provinces are ready now. Does that mean that five provinces are ready to sign an agreement now? If they are ready to sign an agreement, is the agreement of the same character or are the terms of that agreement the same as those in the one that was signed with the province of Ontario, or are there modifications? Are some of the schemes of some of the provinces less comprehensive than others? If they are less comprehensive, are the

I have one passing observation to make. I hope the minister will tell us one thing. He says that there are five provinces willing to enter the scheme by July 1 and he talks about the agreement with Ontario. Will the minister tell us the extent to which the provinces have accepted that portion of the federal offer dealing with diagnostic services? When I had to do with this measure last the province of Ontario was not prepared to accept the full proposal put forward by the federal government in the matter of diagnostic services. It was prepared to accept diagnostic services within a hospital but it was not prepared to embark on a scheme of diagnostic services on a wider basis outside a hospital, somewhat analogous to the diagnostic services scheme in the province of Manitoba.
While the minister cannot force any province into an agreement-and I am not suggesting that course-it will be very interesting to know the extent to which the provinces have accepted the full diagnostic services proposal of the federal government. I should have thought that by now it would have been evident to most of the provinces that this was one of the most attractive features of the proposal and certainly one of the most important ones. If here is anything that is needed today in our country,-I am sure the medical doctors in this house would fully concur in what I am saying-it is that the general practitioner should have at his disposal the greatest possible facilities for diagnosis and that the people at large should not have imposed upon them unnecessary costs of diagnosis that can only be taken care of by the acceptance of the diagnostic services program that was envisaged in the diagnostic services proposal which is now part of the measure before the house.
This is an important measure. It is one to which the previous government attached a great deal of importance. It is a measure which I think all of us on all sides of the house are anxious to see proceeded with as quickly as possible. We shall await with great interest further details which the minister may give. I hope he will be able to tell us that not only are we going to have an agreement that will see in being a scheme with the province of Ontario by July 1 and schemes in preparatory stages with some other provinces, but that by that time, as a result of the introduction of this measure, in co-operation with the provinces we shall see the beginning of a truly nation-wide scheme

of hospital insurance in this country, a measure which I believe will prove to be of the greatest value to the people of Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, last Saturday, May 24, I had the privilege of celebrating my 41st birthday. This measure which is introduced today, in respect of this first faltering step, is going to succeed in cutting six months off the 40 years that it has taken to try to reach completion. In following the history of this health insurance program, or lack of it, down through the years I cannot help wondering whether the fact that we have had two elections in the last year has not had a good deal to do, both with the measure in its original form and with the amendment that is proposed today. Possibly, with regard to the rough and rocky road to health insurance in this country, it might be better if we had elections every six months.

In my view it is simply another of the ragtag and bobtail measures which seem to be the pattern of this government. Apparently the present government is no different from the one it succeeded. It is not bringing in any great new measures but is seeking to patch up the Liberal program with a little amendment here and another little amendment there. The only difference between the present government and the former administration is in the ability of the Prime Minister to convince the people that it is different through the highly developed sense of dramatics with which he has been richly endowed. He appears to be a much better salesman than was the former government in presenting to the people of Canada the program the Liberals started, with only minor alterations.
Hospital Insurance Act
The musty pages of Hansard are filled with words describing the history of health insurance in Canada. I do not intend to deal in any detail with the many chapters and volumes of statements that have been recorded in Hansard in the course of the last 40 years with regard to the subject of national health insurance. I would, however, like to make a resume of a few of the highlights commencing, as I said, with 1919. Mind you, we have come close to achieving it on a number of occasions.
In 1941 the then minister of pensions and national health held a meeting of all the health authorities and interested persons. In 1942 an advisory committee was formed. In 1943 the government struck the House of Commons committee which reported and presented a draft bill in detail. In 1944 a conference was held with representatives of all the provinces. The speech from the throne in the years 1944 and 1945 dealt with the question of health insurance. Four definite proposals were set out in 1945. Of course, many of us can recall the election campaign of that year, when many people in Canada got the impression all that was necessary to have a national health insurance program immediately was to reelect the Liberal party.

The measure before us does not make provision for the kind of health insurance program that was promised and outlined by the Liberals in 1919, but is merely a modified and limited form of hospital insurance with all manner of strings and ropes attached. It is not a health plan as is enjoyed by the citizens of Great Britain. It is not a health plan such as I understand has been enjoyed by the citizens of Germany since 1874 or thereabouts. It is not even a hospital insurance plan such as has been enjoyed by the people of the province of Saskatchewan since 1945 and which I have been told by members of the medical profession is the best hospital insurance plan on the North American continent.
As was mentioned by the hon. member for Essex East, there is no provision at the present time for tuberculosis or mental illness contained in the measure before us. In fact, if one can believe the reports of the federal-provincial conference held last year we were given to understand that at that time the Prime Minister advised that the federal government would advance the money to take care of patients suffering from these two illnesses but it would be deducted from other grants made to the provinces.

speechtext:
It is also extremely interesting to observe the stand taken by various political parties on this question of a health insurance program down through the years. I think I can safely say that the party with which I am associated is the only one which has taken a consistent stand on this question through the years. If one has time to go back through Hansard one is amazed to see who was on which side at what particular time.
Although some may have held different views at various times, the fact remains that no party today opposes the idea of a national health insurance plan, but I must point out that there are people and organizations in Canada who are actively and vigorously fighting against such a measure. The amazing part of it is that the people who are opposed today and those who have fought it down through the years are without exception people who believe in insurance. They believe in insuring their cars, their homes and their lives. They believe in insuring everything but their health, which in my opinion is the most important of these, whether taken on an individual or a national basis.
Let us examine for a moment who is opposed to the national health insurance plan and suggests that it is an abominable thing. I submit that the majority of opposition to an

insurance plan today is centred around the insurance companies, which, even while they oppose a measure of this kind, attempt to sell a personal health insurance plan. This leads me to believe they are not too much interested in the health of individuals in this country but are keenly interested in the dividends earned by their companies.
It has been said, and possibly it is true, that certain doctors in this country are opposed to health insurance on a national basis. I submit that this may be due to their having been subjected to the vast volume of propaganda against national health insurance plans which has been circulated.
It had been called state medicine. We have been told that doctors are going to become civil servants and so on. Many of us know, by watching similar plans in operation in other countries, that such is not the case. These suggestions are nothing more than propaganda.
We have been told that these plans are too costly, and that they would be abused by certain individuals. But, I would ask, what has ever come about that has not been abused by certain individuals? Parliament itself was subjected to abuses at one time, but that does not mean we should abolish parliament. The fact is that regardless of how good a plan you have, certain people will abuse it. The fact remains that it should not be stopped on that ground when it is going to bring benefit to the vast majority of the people.
With regard to the assertions that the plan will be costly, I wonder if we have made a true assessment of the cost of sickness in the past. I wonder if we have included the cost represented by bills which many thousands of doctors have lying unpaid in their studies because the patients they treated were unable to discharge them. I wonder if we have taken into consideration the lost life savings of people who have been stricken by illness; the homes that have been lost, the businesses that have been ruined through no fault of the owners. Above all, have we taken into consideration the cost imposed by the blight of ill health on our nation. I wonder whether there is any method by which we could assess the cost involved in these directions.
I submit that the health of the citizens of this country is something that should not be measured on a profit basis. Regard should not be paid to whether it is profitable or not to embark on such a course, but rather, to whether it is in the interest of the citizens as a whole to deal with this problem. We are told by those opposed to this plan that it

is not really necessary because so many people have proven that they can insure themselves. The fact remains, however, that people who need help most are not insured at all. Many of the plans in effect at the present time are so designed that in effect they will insure you only if you do not need the insurance.
This government has at the present time almost unlimited power. With its huge majority it is able to do practically whatever it wishes. I suggest it should take a much broader view of the need for health insurance in this country and not take these niggling little steps in the right direction. I agree it may be more suitable for propaganda purposes to take one step at a time and, I will add, full propaganda value has been derived from the step we are taking today. It was announced before the election and during the election, and now we have the job of taking this step which so many people thought had already been taken.
If this government fails to implement health insurance on a national basis in this country the only conclusion I can draw is that they are not so much interested in the health of this country as they would be, possibly, in the business of some of their friends. Progress along this line can no more be held up than it can along the line of automation in this country. The time must come finally when health insurance will become a reality here. Meanwhile, there is no reason why we should let people make as much money as they can for as long as they can. If the measure before us today is all the government can offer I suggest that they should not look upon it with pride but hang their heads in shame when they face the people of this country.

the second reading of Bill No. C-3, an act to amend the Criminal Code (capital punishment).
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have been interested in this question of capital punishment for a great many years. My attention was first drawn to this subject some 22 years ago at a time when I was a member of the legislative assembly of the province of British Columbia.
It was authoritatively reported to me at that time that three men in our province who were guilty of homicide had all been dropped from the trap door at the same time, and as one of the men was lighter than the other two and was in between the other two he was held up by the others and his neck was not broken, with the result that he died a gruesome death by strangulation.
In endeavouring to investigate this matter through the medium of the legislature of British Columbia I was told by the then attorney general of the province that before speaking on the subject of capital punishment I should have a full knowledge from a lengthy study of the question and also that I personally should see a man hanged. Gruesome as that second proposal was, if that was a necessary part of my education on this subject I decided that I would see a man hanged; and so a few weeks later I saw a young man brought to a legal death through a trapdoor at Okalla prison farm in British Columbia because he had been the driver of the getaway car from a bank holdup in which the teller was shot. I mention that as my introduction to this subject.
In the course of those 22 years I have done my utmost to obtain a full knowledge of this question of capital punishment or the abolition of capital punishment. I think I am safe in saying that that education reached its culmination when I had the privilege of being a member of the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on the question of capital and corporal punishment. I believe I am safe in saying that there are only three of us still in this house who were among the 17 members of parliament appointed to that joint committee.
In the course of that 22 years and with the knowledge I acquired as a result of being a member of that joint committee I can only come to the conclusion that nowhere can

Criminal Code
I find a good and solid argument for the retention of capital punishment. The only arguments that I have heard put up in favour of capital punishment are, first, that it is a deterrent to further homicide and criminality.
I maintain that that cannot be proved.
There is another argument used by many, namely that capital punishment is a protection for the police force of a country. I maintain that that claim cannot be proved. I have been forced to come to the conclusion that capital punishment is retained for only one of two purposes, either retribution or revenge, and they are not good grounds for the maintenance of legal death because of homicide.
Every one of us has the most heartfelt sympathy for and understanding of the feelings of the relatives and the friends of those who are the victims of murder. Even with that feeling and that understanding, I believe we have to delve a great deal farther in order to decide whether or not we should retain it in this country.	.
I should like to present to the house what I feel are good, substantial and factual reasons why we should most seriously consider the abolition of capital punishment in this country. Proud as we all are of our country, we must admit that there are other countries that are humanitarian, that are Christian, that are civilized and that are modern in their approach to justice and social consciousness. If we examine some of the countries outside of Canada what do we find? May I give a few examples.
In Finland there has been no execution since 1826; capital punishment was abolished in 1949. In Belgium the last execution took place in 1863, except for one case during the 1914-18 war, and capital punishment was abrogated by disuse. In Holland there has been no execution since 1860; capital punishment was abolished in that country in 1870. There has been no execution in Norway since 1876; capital punishment was abolished in 1905. It was abolished in Portugal in 1867. There has been no execution in Rouma-nia since 1838, and it was abolished in that country in 1952. I am just giving illustrations from some of the countries of the world. At the same time I suppose I should comment on the country to the south of us.
In the United States of America capital punishment was abolished in Michigan in 1847; in Wisconsin in 1853; in Maine in 1887; in Minnesota in 1911; in Rhode Island in 1853; and in North Dakota in 1895. Now to be absolutely candid and honest, and I always want to be that, I think I should also mention that in addition to those states in the United States there were 10 other states that abolished capital punishment and brought

it back in later years; but there are still the original states that I mentioned that are abolitionist states in the United States. In addition, there are some 17 countries in central and South America that have abolished capital punishment, going back as far as 1863.
I think we lay a good foundation in considering this matter if we recognize what has happened in so many other countries, going back in many instances over a century. We also must recognize that there are many countries that still have capital punishment. The question obviously and naturally arises, what is the comparison in the homicidal rates between abolitionist countries and nonabolitionist countries? To the best of my knowledge there has been only one comparison table ever produced on this matter and that was the one put out by the United Nations in their demographic year book in 1952. They presented a rate table showing comparisons for the year 1948 as between the homicide rate per 100,000 of population in 11 countries that still have the death penalty and in 15 countries that have abolished the death penalty. Here are the comparative figures as supplied by the United Nations. Among the countries that had the death penalty there are such countries as El Salvador, Canada, the United States, New Zealand, Scotland, Ireland, England and Wales, and so on. The highest rate of homicide was in El Salvador where it was 44.3 per 100,000 population. The lowest rate was in England and Wales, being 0.5 per 100,000 population.
Turning to the countries that have abolished the death penalty we have such countries as Colombia, Finland, Portugal, Belgium, Denmark, Switzerland, Sweden, Norway and The Netherlands. There we find that Colombia has the highest rate, 15.9 per 100,000 population and the Netherlands has the lowest rate, 0.4 per 100,000 population. So it can be shown that there is no considerable differentiation in homicide rates as between abolitionist and non-abolitionist countries.
In referring to such a table I should like to make it clear how it is not to be considered and I think I can do that best by reading an excerpt from evidence given to the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on this matter by Professor Thors-ten Sellin, one of the outstanding penologists of the world. When he appeared before the joint committee he referred to the table and had this to say as found at page 724 of the proceedings of the committee:
This table is not presented with any suggestion that it illustrates the virtue of using or not using the death penalty. It does not and cannot do so. What it illustrates is that countries with high

rates of homicides equally like or dislike this penalty, and so do countries with low homicide rates. Behind these two divergent policies there obviously lie other reasons than the extent of criminality of a homicidal nature, reasons of an intangible character, connected with the political, economic and social structure of a country, and buttressed by traditions protected by sentiments and beliefs which apparently are not influenced by the level of criminality.
Having introduced the subject in the way I have by reference to other countries and states of the United States and by giving comparative figures of homicide rates in abolitionist and non-abolitionist countries, I think, Mr. Speaker, that you would rightfully expect me to deal with the situation in our own country. Those members who have not read the evidence of the committee may be interested in knowing that the then minister of justice supplied the committee with information that between 1930 and 1949, 407 persons were sentenced to death in Canada and of those 407 there were 220 who were executed.
This makes it clear that even since 1930 there has been, through the medium of the Department of Justice and the clemency of the crown a progressive desire to get away, if possible, from the death sentence. I know that a lot of people have the idea that if a person once commits homicide the best thing to do is to get rid of him by breaking his neck and that such persons are not capable of rehabilitation. I think those who hold that view do not know the actual facts. In a great majority of cases murder is committed in the heat of emotion, of passion, of fear, of temper, and it is often possible to rehabilitate such a person into a useful social life.

subsequently released on ticket of leave.
It is understandable that the 17 members of the House of Commons and 10 members of the other place who formed the committee were interested in knowing what happened to those 71 and the Department of Justice through the medium of the R.C.M.P., I believe, was able to give us a factual report. The evidence was that of those on ticket of leave only one got into serious trouble again.
Criminal Code
As a matter of fact, he committed another murder. We only have one in the known history of such cases and this time he had his neck broken. I should like to read one paragraph in this regard found in the transcript of the proceedings of the joint committee. On page 699 of volume II of the proceedings there is the following:
Nearly all the ticket of leave holders are described in recent post-release reports from R.C.M.P. and social agencies as accepted, re-established and even respected citizens. The special achievements of particular individuals cannot be detailed without identification. A very small number appear to have made only a marginal adjustment.
I raise the issue in this way in an endeavour to cover in a factual manner the statistics and facts as they can be found in other countries and as we know them to the best of our knowledge in Canada. I am not in any way expressing any drooling sentimentality for criminals and especially for murderers. If a person is a danger to society then he should and must be incarcerated where he can no longer be a danger to society. If it is possible to rehabilitate him then he should be rehabilitated. But the key point which I think can be gathered from the facts I have given, facts that can be found in the records of countries throughout the world and the records of our own House of Commons, is that there is no differentiation in the rate of homicides because a country is abolitionist or non-abolitionist.
I should now like to deal for a moment with the argument that the death penalty is a protection for our police forces. We all want to do everything possible for the protection of our police. We want to make sure that we do not take any action that will endanger them. I think I can assure the house that this matter received a great deal of consideration not only by myself but by all members of the House of Commons and Senate on the committee. We were amazed to find that no study, of which there was any knowledge, had ever been made with respect to whether or not capital punishment was a protection for the police forces of the country. Even Professor Thorsten Sellin, whom I mentioned a moment ago, said that he had never heard of such a study. He had never even thought of it but as it was a most interesting factor he undertook, as head of the department of sociology and criminology of the University of Pennsylvania, to have a study made and it was made. It was made in the United States, and I quote from the report which was sent to us some 18 months later by the professor. I quote from page 719 of the committee proceedings:
In the author's seminar in criminology at the University of Pennsylvania during the academic year 1954-55, several studies have been carried on

Criminal Code
relating to various aspects of capital punishment. One of these studies was specifically designed to secure data on the comparative risk of a policeman's being injured or killed by a criminal or suspect using a lethal weapon.
During the middle of December, 1954, a letter was mailed to police departments in all cities with more than 10,000 population according to the census of 1950. This letter asked for data to be supplied on two schedules. One of these requested information, year by year beginning with 1919 and ending with 1954, on each case of a wounding or a killing of a member of the police department by a lethal weapon in the hands of a criminal or a suspect. A brief description of each incident was requested indicating, if possible, the nature of the offence involved.
As a result of this, the first study of its kind made by the University of Pennsylvania under the direction of Professor Sellin, the seminar came to a certain conclusion. Since my time is limited I cannot go into it in detail, but that conclusion is found on page 723 of our transcript of evidence.
It is obvious from an inspection of the data that it is impossible to conclude that the states which have abolished the death penalty have thereby made the policeman's lot more hazardous. It is also obvious that the same differences observable in the general homicide rates of the various states are reflected in the rate of police killings.
In drawing my remarks on this bill to a conclusion I hope that even in such a short time I have been able to bring to the attention of hon. members the experiences of the world, abolitionist and non-abolitionist countries and states; the record obtained by the United Nations and the world's leading penologists of comparative rates of homicide; the factfinding on the position of capital punishment or the abolition of capital punishment as regards the protection of our police forces, to an extent that there will be a recognition that it is time in Canada we moved ahead with modern thought, recognizing that the basis of justice and law in our country should not be that of retribution and revenge but should be that of the protection of society at all times and rehabilitation where such is possible. It should be mentioned that in the report made by the joint committee to this house there was not a recommendation that capital punishment be abolished in Canada at this time.
I know I am correct in saying that in the three years the committee met I did not miss a single meeting, so I think I know the feeling of the members of that committee. I believe I am not being unfair at all when I say that the general consensus of that committee was that they recognized that capital punishment in Canada would have to go; that it would go, but that it might be a few years before action is taken. They did not believe the majority of people in Canada were yet in favour of it. It is my own personal belief that when you have a recognition that a

change is going to be made, a recognition that it should be made, then the members of the House of Commons have a responsibility to give leadership and to take action when that is the correct thing to do.
I want to conclude by saying that I have reached these conclusions only after some 22 years of study of the matter and after an honest evaluation of all the factors and a real understanding of what it means to the family of the victim of a murderer. I cannot help but come to the decision that we should now demonstrate our progress in the field of penology and abolish capital punishment. I feel that if a vote of the people of Canada were taken many might be surprised by the number who would favour abolition. Of course, this is only my own surmise. I do know that editorially almost every newspaper in Canada has consistently called upon the government of Canada to abolish capital punishment. I hope that this matter will not be considered along party lines, but from an individual viewpoint. I hope it will be possible for members to support second reading of this bill, and that we can take what I maintain would be a forward step in our system of penology in this country.

speechtext:
It is true that many faces have disappeared from the ranks of the opposition and that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) has had, through his constructive policies, the heads of a good portion of the former opposition. However, the hon. member for Vancouver East here raises a problem of

criminal law which has been prominently featured in many countries during the last few years. In Canada this question has formed the subject matter of an extensive study by a committee of the Senate and House of Commons.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, the bill introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) does not seem to meet at all the wishes of the Canadian people. As far as 1 am concerned, I must say that I have never been approached with the request that capital punishment be abolished. To my knowledge, no such request has ever been_ submitted; moreover, after consulting several of my colleagues, I must also say that the Canadian population does not seem particularly anxious to call for the suppression of capital punishment.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, this is a premature request. The bill submitted by the hon. member for Vancouver East constitutes, in fact, a very delicate requirement, as the provisions of the Criminal Code are the result of the accumulated wisdom of our legislators not only over the years, but over the centuries.	[DOT]
The request is made today that a particular-let us say capital-clause of the criminal code be abolished. Well, we should venture on this ground with great caution and with extreme consideration so as to determine whether such demand fits in with our way of life and agrees with public opinion.
At present, our criminal code defines three types of capital offences: treason, piracy and murder proper. However, for all practical purposes, for many years, Mr. Speaker, capital punishment in this country has had to be applied only in cases of murder, thank God!
The criminal code also provides under section 206 the type of punishment to be inflicted in case of murder, and it is death. It also provides under section 642, the method of execution which, in our country, is hanging.
It must not be assumed that present legislators, any more than their predecessors, have lightly allowed such a drastic provision to be written into our criminal code. Far from it, and that is why they have included provisions whereby the carrying out of the death penalty is accompanied by solemn precautions, to avoid miscarriages of justice and to ensure proper regard for human feelings.
That is why, it is a principle of our criminal law that the accused is presumed innocent until proven guilty by the crown. We should pay tribute to our lawmakers for
57071-3-46J
Criminal Code
thus preserving the full possibilities of the human being by making it incumbent upon the state to prove guilt.
Things are quite different in France, for instance, where the person under arrest is considered guilty until proven innocent. There is all the difference between inquisitorial and accusatory procedure. Our legislators so fully realized the seriousness of capital punishment that they wanted the preparations leading to a trial and the proceedings after a trial to be surrounded with truly exemplary judicial caution.
Moreover, by virtue of section 658, the condemned person may always invoke the royal prerogative of pardon. In addition, section 596 of the Criminal Code provides that the Minister of Justice can order a new trial. Also, the governor in council may commute the death sentence to life imprisonment.
From 1920 to 1949 out of 597 death sentences, there were only 313 executions, which shows that the lawmakers' legislative precautions have allowed for a review of the cases, a review of judicial decisions and of the verdicts of the jury. In this way a thorough analysis is made of the motives of the criminal in order to determine whether there are any grounds for commuting the death sentence to a lesser penalty.
The hon. member for Vancouver East spoke a moment ago of a final report brought down in June, 1956, which contains certain arguments for the maintenance of the death penalty. I have no intention, Mr. Speaker, of dealing with this matter in detail and of extracting all that can be extracted from these arguments. However, I do wish to list them briefly so that the house may understand that a number of these conclusions result from sound logic, based on the experience of centuries and on conditions peculiar to the life of this country. This report, among others, decides in favour of the death penalty, as the welfare of the community must come before the welfare of the individual. It states that capital punishment is an efficient deterrent to murder, a just and adequate punishment; it is the wish of the Canadian people and is still less cruel than life imprisonment. It also makes the administration of jails easier and less dangerous. Moreover, the report answers the argument which the hon. member for Vancouver East raised a few moments ago, by saying that capital punishment is a greater protection for our police forces. At page 23 of that report, we find some suggestions.
Obviously, the commission always inspired with a deep sense of justice, decided in favour of the maintenance of capital punishment. It suggests some alleviations in the method of

Criminal Code
execution together with a periodical revision of that important problem by parliament.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, when one speaks of capital punishment it is most difficult to maintain a logical and reasonable opinion because this subjects covers a field where emotions and reason are in conflict. We are apt to ask ourselves if in demanding such a sentence, we are not becoming murderers. On the other hand, in trying to eliminate capital punishment, we discover that it is an excess of sensitivity which makes us wish to do so. We must never lose sight of the fact that the problem of death is a natural one; all of us must eventually face death and we must not show any excess of feeling in this regard. If we really want to mourn those who have disappeared from this life we should instead think of our fellow men who died during war or through accidents of some kind. Individuals who have committed, at times, the most insidious crimes, do not deserve on our part special pity or tenderness.
For many centuries, and in many countries, capital punishment has always been an extraordinary deterrent to murder, and has undoubtedly contributed to suppress the recurrence of crime. Is the criminal not handicapped and limited in the pursuit of his purpose by the menacing spectre of death by hanging? Human nature, deficient and imperfect, is such that in order to become frightened it must face a punishment proportionate to the crime committed.
To suppress capital punishment is almost to tell criminals that they need only fear minor reprimands; it would only serve to increase the number of professional criminals who would not only perfect their crimes but would eventually only see in the grim pursuit of their deeds an element of risk and eventual punishment which could be quite acceptable.
The average criminal, whether he be the perpetrator of a crime of passion or of a professional crime, is somehow rejected by society. A French writer of great renown has declared that he kills for want of imagination. If he were intelligent he would accept the reversals and deceptions of life more willingly and would acquire a moderate philosophy with regard to the emotional changes which the human being must necessarily encounter.
A criminal is an unbalanced and a sick person, led far beyond normalcy by passion and feeling. I am therefore convinced that any easing up in this regard would only contribute to the criminal surrendering himself completely to this unequilibrium and deficiency.
You may be sure that should it be known tomorrow that capital punishment has been

abolished there would be a considerable increase of criminals who would give free course to their feelings of hatred and jealousy. We are, after all, not like other animals. We are reasonable animals. Always a night lamp of conscience shines within us restraining our desires and instincts. In this case, once capital punishment has been abolished, this lamp will not shine again.
Usually those who advocate the abolition of capital punishment suggest that the state or government strengthen its protective system in order to protect the citizens and prevent crime. Does that not constitute, Mr. Speaker, far too heavy an atmosphere for a citizen who, as a free man, needs a certain liberty and, I might add, a certain casualness in his way of living? The policing methods so far introduced in many countries have made man unhappy and have forced him, too often, to move within too limited and inadequate a scope. Moreover, a developed system of policing and complicated protective measures would be most unfair to our Canadian society, as this would mean considerable expense and additional charges to honest people. Why should honest and law-abiding people always paV for the carelessness and turpitude of undesirables who might eventually become fatally dangerous? No, Mr. Speaker, the adoption of such preventive measures would constitute a serious injustice to the majority of our Canadian citizens.
I must admit that whenever this subject is discussed the possibility of a judicial error is mentioned. At first this argument seems to carry a certain weight and we have a tendency to either ignore it completely or become indifferent to it. I will limit myself to one simple observation. How is it that we are so anxious to deplore a judicial error while we almost never complain about the so-called errors caused by life itself? Sickness, for instance, is so much more injurious and detestable, striking indiscriminately left and right, much more so than judicial error. How often do we see the sole support of a family removed from his loved ones through the vagary of a germ or an accident, while nature spares the life of a miserable and useless person.
Moreover, with regard to this argument of the judicial error it must be pointed out that there have been very few such errors through the years. Here in Canada we know of not one single error and should one or two have occurred it would have proved to be, as in many phases of life, the exception which proved the rule.
The retaining of capital punishment in our Criminal Code comes from an instinctive and natural justice. It is the law of the old testament which advocates "An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth". If you kill someone I, or

the society to which I belong, will kill you. This radical menace hanging over man has proved itself to be most effective through the ages. It is a sort of Damocles sword suspended over the heads and consciences of the individual.
Mr. Speaker, I am of the opinion that the actual composition of our Criminal Code, calling for condemnation to death for murder, is the result of the wisdom and experience acquired through time and that therefore section 206 of the Criminal Code should not be amended as long as our habits and institutions so dictate, and as long as public opinion in its great majority does not make such a modification imperative.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) on presenting to this house a very interesting statistical talk on criminology and also express appreciation to the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) for his comments. I, however, find my thoughts travelling two completely divergent paths. First is the natural abhorrence we all have to violent death whether that violence be the legal violence of authority or the illegal violence of the criminal. The second is the responsibility of this parliament to protect the public against wrongdoers. In my thinking I have tried to follow both paths to a conclusion. I have tried to do it without permitting emotions to influence my judgment for I believe the approach to the problem of capital punishment must be an objective one and emotion should have no part in it.
Past parliaments have devoted much time to this problem. Committees of parliament have heard many witnesses both for and against it. There has been no unanimity of opinion. By and large this opinion can be summed up as follows. Those charged with enforcing the law are of the opinion that capital punishment should be retained as a deterrent. Those who oppose this opinion say it is no deterrent, that the person who in the heat of passion slays a fellowman would have done that killing regardless of the law. They say the man who goes out armed with a revolver to commit some illegal act and who uses that revolver during the course of the act is not deterred from using it by the fact that our Criminal Code contains a provision for hanging such offenders. They say that the cold, calculated murder will still be committed whether the penalty for that murder is death or life imprisonment. In other words they argue that capital punishment is not a deterrent and is justified only as a form of punishment. They say its retention in our Criminal Code is justified only if we
Criminal Code
believe in the philosophy of an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. They say, too, that as long as capital punishment remains a provision of the Criminal Code there will remain the possibility that by due process of law we, the people of Canada, may put to death an innocent person. Protagonists of the law say that the Canadian system of administration of justice protects the innocent and is a guarantee against such a miscarriage.
I have opinions on all these arguments. I am not convinced, for instance, that capital punishment is of sufficient value as a deterrent, if that were the only consideration to justify its retention. Neither am I convinced that the administration of justice, as it is practised in Canada, precludes the possibility of an innocent person being convicted. For instance, recently in the Toronto area three youths were convicted of the robbery of a service station and a part of the case against them was an alleged confession they gave to the police. As hon. members may know, I believe the real perpetrator of the crime was subsequently arrested.
I have talked recently with a man who, in the course of his duties has had to be in attendance at three executions. I was struck, particularly, by one comment he made. This was that any person who had ever witnessed a fellowman being put to death by the due process of law would no longer be a proponent of capital punishment, a process which he described as a degrading and brutal revenge extracted by society from the wrongdoer. I make no comment on this except to say that the man whose opinion I quote is a man in whose judgment I have a great deal of confidence.
If, as is claimed, capital punishment is a deterrent to murder, I often ask myself: why do we not take full advantage of the opportunity that hanging provides to hold up the malefactor as an example to as many persons as possible. For instance, in the old days they knew how to exploit such an occasion. The accused person was trundled through the streets to the place of execution in a cart. The scaffold was erected in a plubic square. The condemned man was given an opportunity to speak to the crowds. As many as 40,000 persons attended such public hangings in England. But did this deter those who witnessed the hangings from committing crimes which would make them liable to the same penalty?
Let us take a look at "The History of Capital Punishment" by George Ryley Scott, a book in the parliamentary library I commend to all members. Mr. Scott quotes a writer describing the execution of a man named John Lechler. It was an execution

Criminal Code
attended by thousands of persons. Immediately following that execution, according to the newpaper reports of the day, 28 persons were committed to jail for offences such as murder, larceny, assault and battery, and so forth. In addition, many lost their pocket books and the pickpockets escaped. Bear in mind that in those days the 28 offences committed while the execution was taking place all carried the penalty of execution upon conviction.
If hanging is a deterrent to murder, why would it not be equally a deterrent to other crime? Could we not establish a completely crime-free Canada if we extended the list of crimes for which death is the penalty? For instance, at the time of the great Sir Edmund Burke no fewer than 222 criminal offences were punishable by death. If an accused man shot a rabbit, forged a birth certificate, stole a pocket handkerchief or adopted a disguise, it could mean he would end his life dangling at the end of a hangman's rope. At one assize alone, early in the nineteenth century, 13 persons were sentenced to death for associating with gypsies.
Indeed, the mere intention to commit a crime was, on many occasions, punished with death. But it is established that the incidence of all types of crime in Britain was never higher than during this period when 222 offences carried death as the punishment.
Evidence before the joint committee on capital punishment which reported on June 27, 1956 is still too recent for quotation from it to be necessary, but one thing that has impressed me in the report of that committee is the evidence of Professor Thorsten Sellin, who came to the committee with exact statistics in regard to murders in the United States, both in those states which had abolished the death penalty and in those which had retained it. I am not going to quote these statistics, but his findings definitely were that the incidence of murder was not increased by the fact that the death penalty had been abolished. In fact, all his evidence would seem to support the statement in the preface of Mr. Scott's book to the effect that the only real deterrent in the death penalty lies in its incontrovertible effectiveness in preventing the repetition of a similar crime by the same person.
As a medical man, I find myself in agreement with another submission in Mr. Scott's book. This is that although there are many types of murder and many varieties of murder, this particular offence rarely ranks as a professional crime carried out by professional criminals in a professional manner. Mr. Scott says it may be described as the crime of the amateur, and that most murderers commit the crime only once.
There is no doubt at all in my mind but that the people of Canada are growing away from a desire for justice based on the creed of "an eye for an eye". More and more, I believe, they are looking towards a day when sentences imposed on those convicted of crime will have a double purpose, to restrain the criminal while the process of rehabilitation is being carried on.
As a private person and a medical doctor, I find much in this bill that commends itself to me. But as a member of parliament with a responsibility to the Canadian people I cannot forget that as recently as two years ago a committee of this house and of the other place, after intensive study, brought in a report favouring the retention of the death penalty in cases of capital offences. Without a greater opportunity for study, and without the benefit of the expert evidence that that committee had before it, I cannot, at this time, vote in favour of a measure which would nullify the recommendations of a committee of this house made such a short time ago.
I believe the time will come when Canada will abolish the death penalty as the punishment for murder. But I do not believe it should be abolished by the motion of a private member on the floor of the house. The procedure, I suggest, should be the procedure of the twenty-second parliament, and any action taken should follow intensive study by a joint committee and a favourable recommendation to this house by that committee. To the end that we may evoke one of the finest and most effective deterrents based on justice and hope for our fellow citizen who may find himself in the unfortunate position of a murderer.

subtopic: LAW OF THE SEA-CANADIAN RESOLUTION AT UN
speechtext:
1.	Did the Canadian delegation at the recent United Nations conference on the law of the sea sponsor a resolution recommending that all states should, pending the outcome of further conferences and discussions, refrain from extending the limit within which they claimed exclusive fishing rights?
2.	If so, what was the outcome of this draft resolution?
Answer by: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
1. Shortly before the conclusion of the United Nations conference on the law of the sea and immediately after the plenary session of the conference failed to adopt any of the proposals put forward concerning the breadth of the territorial sea or the establishment of a contiguous fishing zone, the Canadian delegation, together with the delegations of Australia, Ceylon and Ghana, put forward a proposal concerning the reconvening of the conference. This joint proposal, after referring to the fact that the conference had "already adopted conventions and other instruments with regard to all the matters referred to it with the exception of the breadth, of the territorial sea and the extent of the fishing rights which should pertain to coastal states in the contiguous zone", went on to point out, first, that "it would be contrary to the interests of all states, and could create difficulties in the application of the several conventions and other instruments already adopted by the conference, if agreement is not eventually reached on these important matters", (the breadth of the territorial sea and the establishment of a contiguous zone for fishing rights) and second, that "the prospects of securing general agreement on these two matters would be improved by an adjournment of the discussion of them which would enable the governments of the participating states in the interval to conduct further discussions among themselves". The proposal then called on the conference to take the following action:	(1) "recommend
that all states should, pending the outcome of the adjourned discussions above mentioned, refrain from extending the limits of their territorial sea or the limits within which they claim exclusive fishing rights"; and (2) "request the Secretary General of the United Nations to reconvoke the present conference, at the headquarters of the United Nations, after consultation with the president of the conference and the participating states at the earliest practicable date after the conclusion of the thirteenth session of the general assembly-which will take place this fall-for the purpose of further considering the breadth

Questions
of the territorial sea and the extent of the fishing rights which should pertain to coastal states in the contiguous zone".
2. The joint resolution was not voted upon by the conference. A Cuban resolution which merely requested "the general assembly of the United Nations to study, at its thirteenth session (1958), the advisability of convening a second international conference of plenipotentiaries for further consideration of the
questions left unsettled by the present conference" was submitted to the conference prior to the joint resolution and was consequently voted upon first. The Cuban resolution was adopted by a two-thirds majority vote of the conference, and under those circumstances the president of the conference declared that the proposal co-sponsored by Australia, Canada, Ceylon and Ghana would not be put to the vote.

Monday, June 2, 1958
